Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled impressive progress in understanding explicit semantic structure, such as syntactic parsing, semantic role labeling, and coreference resolution. However, more subtle aspects of meaning, such as implicit arguments, remain challenging due to their indirect relationship with the surface structure of text. Implicit arguments arise when an event is described, and a passive participant is implied but not explicitly mentioned. For example, in the sentence “The man hit the table,” the implicit argument  “the table”  is the patient of the event, even though it is not syntactically linked to the verb “hit” through typical grammatical roles like object or subject. Identifying these implicit participants—also known as implicit arguments—is critical for applications such as event understanding, semantic inference, and downstream tasks like question answering and machine reading comprehension. Unlike explicit arguments, implicit arguments are not directly encoded in sentence syntax or morphology, making them difficult to model using traditional linguistic features alone. Classical approaches, often rule- or feature-based, have attempted to capture these implicit connections, typically requiring carefully curated knowledge bases, large annotated corpora, and handcrafted features. However, these methods suffer from limited scalability and portability across domains, and are evaluated on small datasets, as large-scale high-quality annotated corpora for implicit argumentation are rare. Moreover, such methods struggle to model the nuanced context and coherence patterns necessary to infer implicit roles. With the rise of deep learning, there is a growing opportunity to move beyond feature engineering by leveraging models that can learn rich contextual representations from large volumes of unannotated text. A key insight in this work is that implicit argument prediction can benefit from large-scale language modeling by treating it as a cloze-style task. In contrast to prior approaches that rely on manually annotated training examples, we argue that a cloze task enables the generation of gold-standard training data at scale, where models are asked to predict the missing entity that is an implicit argument of a given event. This framing not only allows the use of automatically generated data—thereby overcoming annotation bottlenecks—but also aligns with the way implicit information is often evaluated in tasks like the Winograd Schema Challenge, where commonsense reasoning is critical. Our model architecture is based on a deep learning framework that integrates narrative coherence and entity salience from the surrounding textual context. By using contextualized embeddings, the model can learn to capture the subtle cohesiveness of event descriptions and infer implicit participants based on global discourse structure, rather than just relying on local syntactic cues.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) from electronic medical records (EMRs) plays a pivotal role in medical text mining, facilitating tasks such as diagnosis coding, drug discovery, patient monitoring, and more. Despite its importance, NER in the medical domain is particularly challenging due to the highly specialized and domain-specific vocabulary used across different clinical specialties. Clinicians in cardiology, oncology, pediatrics, and other fields use varying terminologies and abbreviations, tailored to the needs and conventions of their specific disciplines. This discrepancy, combined with the high cost and effort required for annotation, poses significant barriers to the development of generalizable medical NER systems. Most existing NER models are domain-specific, trained on annotated data from a single specialty and thus unable to generalize to other clinical subfields without reannotation. While transfer learning has shown promise in bridging this gap by leveraging knowledge from pre-trained models on large, general-purpose text or labeled data from related domains, it often fails to account for the nuanced, label-specific differences that exist between specialties. Current methods in transfer learning typically treat all classes uniformly and do not consider the structural or contextual distinctions among the entity labels, which can lead to suboptimal performance when applied to cross-specialty settings. In this paper, we introduce  Label-aware Double Transfer Learning (La-DTL) , a novel framework designed to address these challenges in cross-specialty medical NER. Our approach is motivated by the observation that both feature representation and model parameters are instrumental in adapting an NER system from one specialty to another. To this end, La-DTL incorporates two innovative label-aware components that target improvements in both stages of the transfer process. First, we propose  label-aware Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD)  as a novel method for aligning feature representations across different specialties. Unlike traditional domain adaptation techniques that treat all classes the same, the label-aware MMD ensures that the feature distributions for each entity class are aligned independently, preserving the discriminative power of the label space in the transferred domain. Second, we introduce a  label-aware parameter transfer  approach based on a theoretical upper bound on the error rate. By focusing the parameter sharing and adaptation on label-specific components, we ensure that the transferred model retains strong label-specific performance in the target domain. We evaluate the effectiveness of La-DTL on 12 cross-specialty NER tasks, spanning various medical subfields such as cardiology, oncology, and radiology.

The task of document summarization—generating concise and coherent abstractions of the content of a longer document or set of documents—is a central challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP). One of the most widely used evaluation frameworks for summarization systems is the Text Analysis Conference (TAC), which organizes shared tasks to assess the performance of both human and machine summarization systems. TAC employs a ranking approach that relies on an average score over a collection of document sets to determine the relative quality of summarization systems participating in the task. These scores are typically derived from human and system annotations, with the aim of distinguishing high-performing systems. However, the effectiveness of the average score as a ranking metric has not been rigorously evaluated from a statistical perspective. In this paper, we investigate whether the standard TAC scoring method is appropriate for comparing summarization systems, particularly in the context of distinguishing between human and machine outputs. A key challenge in summarization evaluation is the variability in human annotations, which often leads to agreement issues and makes interpretation of statistical significance difficult. Additionally, using the average score hides important distributional differences between systems and may not capture systematic patterns or domain-specific strengths and weaknesses. We propose an alternative ranking method that takes into account the variability in evaluation scores across different document sets. Our approach incorporates more robust statistical techniques, such as ordinal regression and bootstrapped ranking, which allow for a more nuanced comparison of systems. Specifically, we demonstrate that our method not only retains the overall ranking of systems but also provides greater statistical confidence in differentiating between human and machine summarization outputs, which are known to have distinct patterns in performance and reliability. To evaluate our approach, we conduct an extensive analysis on data from recent TAC summarization tasks, comparing the rankings produced by the traditional average score with those generated by our proposed method. The results indicate that the new method leads to more accurate and consistent rankings, particularly when distinguishing systems that are close in performance. Furthermore, we find that it is more sensitive to the relative strengths of human versus machine systems, offering insights that are valuable for task organizers, system developers, and researchers alike. This work contributes to the ongoing effort to improve the reliability and interpretability of summarization evaluation. By addressing the statistical limitations of the current ranking approach, we take a step toward more precise and fair comparisons of summarization systems, especially in contexts where the source of the summary (human or machine) is a key consideration.

The integration of vision and language represents one of the grand challenges in artificial intelligence, aiming to achieve a deep understanding of multimodal input—specifically, the ability to interpret and reason across images or videos and natural language. Over the last two years, this area has experienced a dramatic surge in research activity, driven by advances in deep learning, greater computational power, and, importantly, the availability of large-scale multimodal datasets. These datasets have not only enabled the development of novel models but have also facilitated benchmarking, comparison, and a deeper understanding of the capabilities and limitations of vision and language systems. Hence, understanding the characteristics of these datasets is crucial for guiding future research, enabling fair evaluations, and identifying areas requiring further development. In the past, datasets for vision and language research were often small, limited in scope, and developed within specific research communities. Today, the landscape has changed, with a proliferation of datasets covering a wide range of tasks, modalities, and complexity levels. These include, but are not limited to, tasks such as image captioning, visually grounded question answering, visual reasoning, and video captioning. While the diversity of available datasets has accelerated progress in the field, it also presents challenges in selecting appropriate data for specific research goals, ensuring consistency in evaluation, and identifying opportunities for improvement. As a result, there is a pressing need to systematically examine the available corpora, identify their commonalities and distinctions, and establish criteria for evaluating their quality and utility. In this paper, we survey the most prominent datasets for vision and language research and propose a set of quality metrics for their assessment. These metrics are based on linguistic complexity, visual complexity, modality alignment, coverage, diversity, and annotation quality. Using these dimensions, we classify and categorize the datasets, analysing key trends in their design and features. Our findings reveal a shift toward increased language complexity and the incorporation of abstract concepts and reasoning in more recent datasets. This evolution reflects the field's maturation, as researchers move beyond basic captioning and object recognition tasks to address richer, more challenging problems. By providing a comprehensive overview of current vision and language datasets and their alignment with the evolving research landscape, this paper aims to support researchers in selecting, evaluating, and developing multimodal datasets. Additionally, by highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of existing resources, we identify gaps and opportunities for future work, such as the need for datasets covering underrepresented languages, cultures, and domains, as well as those addressing ethical and societal concerns.

Grammar induction from raw text is one of the foundational challenges in computational linguistics, with significant implications for natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as parsing, generation, and machine translation. Unlike supervised grammar induction, which benefits from manually annotated training data, unsupervised induction requires the system to discover syntactic structure without any explicit guidance. This task is particularly difficult because the space of possible grammatical structures is vast, and the system must not only reconstruct valid syntactic patterns but also maintain grammatical generalization across diverse sentence structures. Over the decades, researchers have explored a variety of models and algorithms to address this issue, from probabilistic context-free grammars to more complex dependency-based and phrase structure grammars. Among these, dependency grammar induction has gained increasing attention due to its well-defined graphical structure, which explicitly models the head-dependent relationships in sentences. While substantial progress has been made in this domain, most existing approaches employ overly simplistic grammatical models in comparison to the rich structural representations of supervised systems. This limitation has hindered the ability of unsupervised dependency grammars to capture the nuanced syntactic variation present in natural language. In this paper, we address these limitations by presenting an unsupervised approach to dependency grammar induction using   Tree Substitution Grammars   (TSGs). Tree Substitution Grammars are an extension of standard grammatical frameworks that allow for the repeated substitution of subtrees – i.e., reusable fragments of syntactic structure – during the parsing process. This capacity enables TSGs to model larger and more complex syntactic fragments compared to traditional dependency grammar models, which typically rely on binary parent-child relationships. By incorporating tree substitution, our approach aims to more accurately model the recursive and hierarchical nature of syntactic dependencies in natural language. However, the increased expressiveness of TSGs introduces a significant challenge: without careful prior assumptions, the model can overfit the data by generating an excessive number of complex and possibly spurious tree productions. To address this, we introduce a   hierarchical non-parametric Pitman-Yor process   prior that biases toward grammatical simplicity. The Pitman-Yor process is a powerful Bayesian non-parametric tool used in a variety of NLP tasks, known for balancing exploration and exploitation in the discovery of latent structures. Our prior encourages the model to produce a compact grammar with a limited number of tree productions while still maintaining the flexibility necessary to capture the structural diversity of the input text. This hierarchical extension allows us to model dependencies at multiple levels of the syntactic tree, constraining the grammar in a principled and data-driven way.

The field of natural language processing (NLP) has experienced remarkable growth and transformation over the past few decades, driven by advancements in deep learning, the availability of large-scale annotated datasets, and the increasing demand for human-computer interaction systems across various domains. Despite these developments and a progressive push toward inclusivity and diversity within the broader field of artificial intelligence (AI), a subtle yet persistent disparity in leadership and representation remains among specific demographics—particularly in authorship of high-impact research and participation in top academic and industry positions. In this paper, we investigate whether such disparities constitute a "glass ceiling"—a structural barrier that disproportionately impacts underrepresented groups within the NLP community. Using a rigorously studied mathematical model for bi-populated networks, we analyze patterns in authorship and citation data across influential NLP conferences and journals since the mid-2000s to uncover the extent of such inequalities and how they evolve over time. The notion of a glass ceiling is often discussed in sociological, organizational, and academic literature in the context of gender and other sociodemographic factors. While prior research has highlighted the importance of diversity in fostering innovation and reducing algorithmic bias, few empirical studies have examined whether such systemic barriers manifest quantitatively in research fields like NLP. Our work is motivated by two observations: first, that NLP, like many STEM disciplines, has historically been male-dominated, and second, that despite increasing efforts to promote inclusivity, the proportion of underrepresented groups in leadership roles in the field has not converged at a level that matches their overall participation at earlier career stages. We hypothesize that structural patterns in NLP research ecosystems—such as citation habits, mentorship opportunities, and peer review biases—contribute to a form of self-reinforcing stratification that limits upward mobility for underrepresented groups. To test this hypothesis, we adapt a mathematical model originally designed to study bi-populated networks in social systems and apply it to datasets that capture authorship and citation patterns within NLP. The model allows us to simulate the evolution of contributions and recognition within the community, based on metrics such as peer evaluation, collaboration frequency, and citation preferences. Using empirical data from NLP conferences such as ACL, NAACL, and EMNLP as well as sustained journal submissions, we identify a significant disparity in the proportion of high-impact work attributed to members of the underrepresented group. Our analysis reveals a consistent trend since the mid-2000s where the visibility and recognition of underrepresented contributors do not scale proportionally with their academic or professional inputs.

The collaborative nature of Wikipedia has made it a vibrant and dynamic source of knowledge, continuously refined by the contributions of its community through document revisions. These edits range from minor corrections to significant content overhauls, and their characterization poses a critical challenge in understanding the evolutionary processes of Wikipedia content, managing quality assurance, and enabling tools that support contributors. Edit category classification is a key task in this domain, aiming to assign predefined categories—such as "spelling error correction," "paraphrase," or "vandalism"—to each edit. Accurate classification not only aids in tracking the nature and trends of content changes but also supports monitoring the quality and trustworthiness of articles, as well as enhancing personalized tools and workflows for editors. A primary challenge in edit classification lies in the diversity and complexity of editing behaviors, especially given the rich surface forms edits can take, the heterogeneity of content, and the absence of canonical or static features. Previous approaches have focused on a mix of raw character-level, lexical, and syntactic features; however, these often fall short in capturing the nuanced intentionality and subtle variations in edit types. Additionally, the classification task is complicated by the need for multi-label categorization, as a single edit can simultaneously belong to multiple categories. In this paper, we introduce a novel set of features tailored for the automatic classification of edit categories in Wikipedia revisions. These features are derived from the differences between two successive document versions, and they capture three core aspects of edits: (1) meta data (e.g., timestamps, user activity history), (2) textual and language properties (e.g., edit size, language complexity shifts), and (3) markup changes (e.g., HTML tag modifications). By integrating these dimensions, we aim to create a richer representation of edit intent that can disentangle the often-overlapping signals across different classes. To evaluate the effectiveness of our feature set, we conduct a supervised machine learning experiment on a corpus of edits derived from the English Wikipedia. Each edit in this corpus is labeled according to a 21-category taxonomy, allowing for a robust assessment of both class-wise effectiveness and overall model performance. Our approach achieves a micro-averaged F1 score of 0.62, which demonstrates strong scalability across a large space of edit types. Additionally, we show that the same model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the related task of fluency edit classification, confirming the generalizability of our feature design.

Question answering (QA) systems have made significant progress in recent years, particularly in handling factoid questions that can be answered through string matching or structured database queries. However, non-factoid questions, which require an understanding of context, subjectivity, and inference, remain a challenging topic in natural language processing (NLP). Among non-factoid questions,  why-questions  are particularly complex as they require deeper reasoning about causal relationships between events or phenomena. A typical why-question tends to ask for an explanation, often linked to a referent event or situation that is either positive or negative in nature. For instance, when someone asks  “Why did the economy improve?”  it is mostly expected that the answer will relate to positive contributing factors, such as policy changes or favorable global conditions. Conversely, if the question is  “Why did the crime rate increase?” , the answer is likely to point to undesirable or negative factors. This paper explores the idea that the sentiment associated with a why-question and its corresponding answer can be leveraged to improve the quality of answer retrieval and ranking in QA systems, particularly for non-factoid questions. While sentiment analysis has been extensively used for text classification and opinion mining, its application in question answering has been limited, especially to non-factoid domains. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that explicitly incorporates sentiment analysis into the context of why-question answering, leveraging the intuition that questions and their answers often share a similar emotional tone or desirability. We propose a method that combines sentiment analysis with semantic word classes to enhance the performance of a QA system in answering why-questions. Semantic word classes are used to capture the meaning or domain-related context of the words involved in the question and the potential answers. By combining sentiment analysis with word classes, we aim to improve the system’s ability to not only match the linguistic content of the question but also understand and align the inferred intent or desirability of the question and the proposed answers. Our experiments are conducted on a large-scale web corpus containing 850 why-questions. The results demonstrate that by incorporating sentiment analysis alongside semantic word classes, we achieve a 15.2% improvement in precision at the top-1 answer over a strong baseline system that topped the Japanese non-factoid QA shared task in NTCIR-6. This improvement highlights the potential of incorporating psychological and context-based cues such as sentiment into QA tasks, particularly for open-domain and non-factoid question types where deep understanding of language and human reasoning is essential.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled refined classification of utterances along ideological or socio-cultural dimensions such as stance—specifically, the degree to which a text aligns with, opposes, or remains neutral on a subject of discussion. Stance classification has grown in significance in domains such as legislative debates, online forums, and social media platforms, where the nuances of linguistic expression can provide insights into public sentiment, political discourse, and community dynamics. A substantial body of research has focused on supervised approaches to stance modeling, ranging from simple text classification techniques to more complex structured prediction algorithms that take into account the interdependencies among labels. Twitter has emerged as a particularly rich dataset for stance classification research, given its unique characteristics: the real-time nature of content generation, the broad spectrum of topics discussed, and the inherently social nature of the platform. The short-form text format, although linguistically sparse and contextually fragmented, presents challenges and opportunities in encoding prior knowledge and leveraging social structures. Existing approaches mostly apply feature-based or deep learning models for individual tweet classification. However, the inherent interactivity of Twitter—through likes, retweets, mentions, and responses—suggests that the collective behavior of users can provide additional contextual signals about stance. In this paper, we propose a weakly supervised relational bootstrapping framework for tweet stance classification, which leverages both textual features and social network information. Traditional supervised approaches often require large, manually annotated datasets, which are problematic in fast-evolving and diverse domains like Twitter. We address this limitation by working in a weakly supervised setting, where only a small set of hashtags or keyphrases are manually annotated to indicate a stance (for instance, a hashtag \#climatechange is associated with a pro-environment stance). Our model extends beyond individual post classification by collectively modeling user and post stances through a graph-structured representation of the social network, integrating latent user stance information with the hierarchical dependencies between tweets and users. Our primary technical contribution is the use of hinge-loss Markov random fields (HL-MRFs) for expressing the latent structure of user and post stances as a joint probabilistic model. By incorporating pairwise and higher-order constraints based on user-subgraph connectivity and textual alignment, we enforce consistency in the predicted stance space. This relational modeling approach not only improves the precision of stance prediction per tweet but also enhances the learning of overall user perspectives.

Language modeling is a core task in natural language processing, aiming to assign probabilities to sequences of words to reflect their likelihood in real language. Traditional approaches, such as n-gram models, rely on capturing local dependencies by conditioning the probability of a word on a fixed-length history of preceding words. While effective in simpler settings, these models often fail to capture hierarchical and structural dependencies that exist in language, particularly those related to syntax and semantics. Recent advances have sought to address these limitations by incorporating contextual and semantic representations, but many still lack a formal mechanism to encode the syntactic structure of sentences explicitly and systematically. In this paper, we propose the Latent Tree Language Model (LTLM), a novel language modeling approach that integrates linguistic structure through the construction of latent trees capturing both syntactic and semantic roles of words in a sentence. Unlike purely surface-based models, LTLM represents the relationships between words in a hierarchical and interpretable form, thereby modeling the complex dependencies that arise from the structural nature of language. At the heart of LTLM are two distinct algorithms for tree inference. The first algorithm is based on Gibbs sampling, a probabilistic method that iteratively adjusts the structure of the tree by relocating nodes in the latent tree space. This algorithm is computationally efficient and suitable for tasks requiring rapid tree generation, though it does not guarantee finding the globally optimal tree. The second algorithm leverages dynamic programming to identify the most probable tree with a high degree of accuracy, albeit at a greater computational cost. Each of these algorithms has its own trade-offs in speed and precision, and we evaluate their effectiveness in modeling natural language under varying constraints. To demonstrate the utility of LTLM, we combine it with the well-established 4-gram Modified Kneser-Ney smoothing model via linear interpolation. The combination allows us to leverage the strengths of LTLM's hierarchical modeling while maintaining the robustness of traditional n-gram baselines. Experiments on both English and Czech corpora reveal that the integration of LTLM achieves up to 46% perplexity reduction for English and 49% for Czech, compared to the standalone 4-gram Modified Kneser-Ney model. These results highlight the significant performance gains that can be achieved by incorporating latent syntactic structures into language modeling. Our model not only improves prediction accuracy but also opens the door to interpretable language modeling where the underlying structure of meaning and syntax can be visualized and analyzed.

Question answering (QA) systems aim to provide accurate and precise answers to user-generated questions by leveraging the information contained in a knowledge base. Traditional approaches to QA rely heavily on natural language text as the primary source of knowledge. While text is a rich and abundant resource, it often requires significant natural language understanding and inference to extract the relevant facts necessary for answering questions. On the other hand, highly-structured knowledge bases, such as those in the form of relational databases or ontologies, enable efficient automated reasoning and precise query answering. However, such structured resources are typically labor-intensive to create and maintain, requiring manual curation or complex automated extraction pipelines. This has led to a long-standing trade-off in QA research: the ease of access and the richness of unstructured textual knowledge versus the efficiency and precision offered by structured knowledge bases. In response, semi-structured knowledge representations, such as tables, provide a promising middle ground. Tables are semi-structured in nature, containing rows and columns with clear relationships, yet they are more flexible and easier to acquire than fully structured databases. Furthermore, the widespread use of tables in documents, both in the web and in academic or industry resources, makes them an accessible and abundant form of knowledge. Despite their potential, research on leveraging tables as knowledge sources for QA has remained relatively under-explored, particularly in the context of training machine learning models that can exploit the structure of tables to perform reasoning and answer questions effectively. In this paper, we explore the use of tables as semi-structured knowledge sources for question answering. We motivate this approach by highlighting how the structure inherent in tables can be leveraged to guide the creation of annotated QA datasets and inform the design of feature-driven models for table-based reasoning. We first present a scalable and efficient method for generating a large dataset of multiple-choice questions by leveraging the structure of tables through crowd-sourcing. Importantly, the alignment between the questions and the table content is automatically inferred from the structure, enabling rich and accurate annotations. Our dataset contains over 9,000 hand-annotated questions, making it one of the largest and most diverse collections of table-based QA examples available. We then present a semi-structured feature-driven question answering model that utilizes tables as a knowledge source. The model incorporates features derived from the relationships between question components and the table cells, such as textual similarity, positional dependencies, and semantic roles.

Parsing is a central task in natural language processing (NLP), enabling syntactic analysis that serves as a foundation for downstream applications such as semantic interpretation and machine translation. Over the years, various algorithms have been developed for efficient and accurate parsing, particularly for languages with relatively simple morphological structures like English. These include well-known frameworks such as probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs), Dependency Parsing models, and lexicalized grammar formalisms like Head-Driven Phrase Structure Grammar (HPSG) and Lexicalized Tree Adjoining Grammar (LTAG). However, as NLP systems expand to support a broader range of languages, the demand for efficient parsing algorithms that handle morphologically rich languages has become increasingly critical. Morphologically rich languages, such as French, Spanish, or Turkish, exhibit a higher degree of inflection and rich surface forms, necessitating parsers that can simultaneously model complex word forms and syntactic structures. The classical LR (Left-to-right, Rightmost derivation) parsing algorithm, originally developed for context-free grammars, is known for its high efficiency, thanks to its bottom-up, shift-reduce approach. While initially limited to context-free grammars, recent research has extended LR parsing techniques to accommodate more expressive grammatical formalisms. In parallel, lexicalized parsing models, such as the lexicalized context-free grammar proposed by Collins (2003) and later augmented with discriminative models (Collins, 2002), have demonstrated strong performance on English and similar languages. These models integrate lexical information directly into the parsing process, allowing for more accurate syntactic predictions by leveraging word-specific patterns. This paper bridges the gap between LR parsing algorithm efficiency and the modeling power of lexicalized grammars by proposing a novel   LR-inspired generalized lexicalized phrase structure parser  . The parser extends LR parsing techniques to handle rich lexical representations suitable for morphologically complex languages. It introduces a structured lexical item representation that captures both the morphological and syntactic properties of words, allowing the parser to make informed decisions during bottom-up derivation. To enhance parsing performance, the parser incorporates a discriminative weighting component (Collins, 2002), enabling it to learn accurate models from training data while minimizing reliance on hand-coded grammatical rules. We evaluate our algorithm on two language datasets: a morphologically rich language (French) and a relatively less complex language (English). Our experimental results show that the proposed parser achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on French parsing tasks while maintaining faster parsing times than existing lexicalized phrase structure parsers. Additionally, the parser's performance on English indicates its potential for generalization across linguistic typologies, confirming the robustness of the LR-inspired parsing framework.

Textbooks play a foundational role in education, serving as structured repositories of knowledge and learning. They are particularly valuable in disciplines like mathematics and science, where abstract concepts often require formalized expression and logical sequencing. Despite their importance, extracting structured, formal knowledge from textbooks remains a challenging task, particularly when aiming to automate problem-solving or reasoning systems. This is especially true in domains like geometry, where the application of theory to problems depends on precise, formalized rules often embedded within prose, examples, and diagrams. Automated systems capable of solving geometry problems require access to formalized axioms and theorems. However, most textbooks present this axiomatic knowledge in natural language, requiring human interpretation for system use. Extracting and encoding this knowledge into machine-readable formats such as horn-clause rules offers a promising path toward building intelligent tutoring systems or reasoning assistants. This paper explores the possibility of automating the harvesting of axiomatic geometry knowledge from textbooks with the goal of improving automated problem-solving performance. We propose a methodology that leverages rich contextual and typographical features in textbooks, such as headings, definitions, examples, and visual formatting, to identify and extract axiomatic knowledge. Given the highly structured and formal nature of geometry, the extraction pipeline takes advantage of the consistency in how axioms are presented and expressed across multiple textbooks. These cross-textbook redundancies and shared sequencing of axioms are exploited to improve extraction accuracy and reduce noise from non-axiomatic content. A key innovation of our approach is the treatment of axioms as first-class entities through their conversion into horn-clause rules—logical implications that can be directly used for automated deduction. By parsing extracted axioms into this format, we enable downstream systems to perform deductive reasoning in novel problem-solving scenarios. The parsed horn-clause rules are integrated into a reasoning engine, which is evaluated on a comprehensive geometry problem-solving task. Our results show that the harvested and formalized axiomatic knowledge significantly improves the accuracy and coverage of geometric problem-solving algorithms. The study demonstrates not only the feasibility of processing textbooks as structured knowledge sources but also the importance of capturing domain-specific formalism in educational content. This approach sets a precedent for extending similar techniques to other domains, promoting the development of scalable and intelligent educational assistants. Through this case study, we highlight a new direction in educational data mining and knowledge extraction, bringing us closer to the vision of machine-aided mastery of structured knowledge.

Natural language processing (NLP) systems rely heavily on treebanks — annotated linguistic corpora that provide syntactic or semantic structures — to train and evaluate a wide range of tasks, from syntactic parsing to semantic role labeling. A core challenge in leveraging treebanks lies in the need for transformations or transductions of their tree structures to adapt them for different use cases, evaluation settings, or research questions. These transformations often require careful specification of how tree nodes and their relationships should be altered or preserved. Unfortunately, much of the current methodology for describing tree transformations in the literature is textual and ad hoc, often leading to ambiguities, inconsistencies, and a lack of reproducibility. This paper addresses these limitations by introducing a flexible, declarative language tailored for expressing tree transductions in the context of natural language treebanks. The proposed transduction language is designed to provide a clean, precise, and concise way to describe operations such as tree pruning, node relabeling, structural reorganization, and feature augmentation. It abstracts away low-level programming details while ensuring that the transformations remain fully implementable without requiring hard-coded logic. This is critical not only for reducing the development time and effort required to perform tree transformations, but also for enabling researchers and practitioners to share, reuse, and validate tree transformation specifications with ease. One of the defining characteristics of our transduction language is its applicability to a broad range of NLP tasks. For instance, it can support the alignment of treebanks differing in syntactic formalism, the normalization of tree annotation variations arising from different parsing technologies, or the generation of alternative tree representations needed for cross-task evaluation. Additionally, it facilitates the specification of domain-specific constraints or transformation rules that are essential when adapting existing datasets to new linguistic phenomena or research scenarios. By providing a unified framework for tree transductions, this language significantly enhances the reproducibility and comparability of NLP experiments. To demonstrate its utility, we present examples of transformations derived from well-known NLP tasks, such as the binarization of trees for processing by recursive neural networks and the conversion of dependency trees to constituent trees. These examples illustrate how the language can encapsulate complex transformation logic in a human-readable format while ensuring the accurate operationalization of that logic in software systems. Our ultimate goal in publishing this work is to spark collaboration within the NLP community. We encourage researchers to use this language, extend its capabilities, and apply it to novel domains and use cases.

The task of constructing parallel corpora is a cornerstone in the development of statistical machine translation (SMT) systems, yet it presents significant challenges due to the high cost and labor required for manual alignment. Traditionally, parallel corpora are compiled by leveraging specialized bilingual resources, such as the Canadian Hansard or the Europarl corpus, which are limited in size and language coverage. As a result, many research and real-world SMT applications remain underserved by the lack of parallel data for under-resourced language pairs. In contrast, comparable corpora—monolingual documents in different languages that are semantically aligned—have served as an alternative data source. Conventional methods often rely on these nonparallel corpora and apply sophisticated sentence alignment and filtering techniques to extract potential parallel sentence pairs. However, these methods are constrained by the properties of the initial comparable data and typically involve multiple intermediate steps, such as document and sentence alignment, which can introduce compounding errors and inefficiencies. This paper presents a novel approach that shifts the focus from comparable to a much broader source: the open Web.Mining parallel data directly from the Web is a significantly more challenging yet promising avenue for large-scale data acquisition. To tackle this challenge, we adopt an end-to-end framework that combines two core components: (1) the formulation of effective search queries using a "Learning to Rank" strategy and (2) the refinement of noisy document pairs through probabilistic alignment using IBM Model 1. The "Learning to Rank" component captures crucial patterns and correlations in the query space to surface highly relevant bilingual content, while the alignment module ensures that only high-quality document pairs are retained. This approach eliminates the need for pre-collected comparable corpora and reduces dependency on domain-specific data sources. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves over traditional parallel data extraction techniques in both quantity and quality. When the mined parallel data are incorporated into a standard phrase-based SMT system, we observe substantial gains in translation performance as measured by BLEU score, with improvements that are both statistically significant and linguistically meaningful. To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive empirical study to address the problem of direct Web-based parallel data mining, and our results indicate that such an approach can serve as a scalable and effective solution to the data scarcity problem in MT. By leveraging the vast and diverse content of the Web, our framework opens new possibilities for building SMT systems for low-resource language pairs in a more automatic and efficient manner.

Recent advancements in natural language generation (NLG) have enabled systems to produce high-quality textual content across a wide range of domains, from weather reports and news articles to legal documents and personalized emails. A fundamental challenge in NLG is the generation of referential forms—expressions that introduce and maintain entities such as  the ECDeer coordinates  or  the conference , often used to guide the reader through the discourse (Reiter and Dale, 2000). While much research has focused on the  how  of reference generation, arguably, there is a growing need to address the  what and when —that is, the decision of which referential form to use in a given context and how this decision can vary to generate text that is both coherent and stylistically diverse. One core concern in referential forms is surface variation—producing multiple expressions for the same entity in a way that is not redundant but supports readability and coherence in discourse (Krahmer et al., 2011). Currently, most generation systems rely on deterministic algorithms, producing the same referential form for the same discourse context and input. While such approaches yield reliable results, they do not reflect the natural variation observed in human language production (Dale and Reiter, 2003). Introducing variation in generated texts is not only aesthetically preferable, but also facilitates user engagement and adaptability to reader expectations (Cherson and Mitchell, 2000; Kallmeyer et al., 2008). Therefore, we propose a shift in the modeling of referential form generation from deterministic to  nondeterministic  approaches that explicitly model variation. This paper presents a novel exploration into developing and evaluating variation models for the choice of referential form in NLG. Specifically, we introduce two statistical models: a Naive Bayes model and a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) architecture. These models are trained to capture and generate referential expressions that vary meaningfully according to contextual, lexical, and structural features of the discourse. Our goal is not only to generate referential forms accurate in terms of their alignment with the content, but also to introduce controlled diversity that reflects realistic variation observed in human-generated text. We evaluate these models using two well-established corpora in the field of reference generation: the VaREG corpus for model training and evaluation, and the GREC-2.0 corpus for final system integration and human evaluation. In a human-judgment experiment, we compare the generated texts with the original references and a random baseline to assess their  coherence  and  comprehensibility .

The task of event extraction involves identifying and structuring information about events mentioned in unstructured textual data, such as news articles, social media posts, and other digital content. Traditionally, event extraction systems have been developed for formal, well-structured genres like news articles, where coherent topic coverage and consistent syntax facilitate the identification of temporal, causal, and hierarchical event relationships. However, the rise of user-generated content on platforms like Twitter and Facebook has posed a significant challenge to existing information extraction systems. Such content is often informal, noisy, and contextually sparse, requiring robust and flexible methods to accurately identify the events described. Social media, in particular, has become a central source of real-time event monitoring, especially for applications such as crisis tracking, supply chain impact analysis, and public opinion surveillance. Despite its potential, event extraction from social media is hindered by the inherent limitations of the content itself, including the use of abbreviations, slang, and incomplete syntax. Existing event extractors designed for traditional news documents tend to perform poorly when directly applied to such data due to the lack of discourse structure and coherence, as well as the dynamic and highly variable vocabulary employed. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces a novel approach to event extraction that leverages cross-genre knowledge to improve the performance of event detection and classification in informal, social media texts. Our key insight is that structured knowledge derived from formal domains – such as newswire content – can be effectively transferred to enrich and support event extraction in unstructured domains. This enrichment process enables the system to capture event patterns and configurations that might be missed in the context-impoverished environment of social media. By incorporating external knowledge sources and building upon a multi-stage modeling framework, our proposed method does not rely on additional training data specific to social media but instead utilizes the structural and semantic richness of cross-genre corpora. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a set of real-world social media messages, achieving an absolute 15% improvement in F-score over the state-of-the-art. This result underscores the importance of knowledge enrichment and cross-genre learning in enhancing event extraction effectiveness in challenging domains. Furthermore, our approach does not require additional annotated data or domain-specific modifications, making it scalable and adaptable to a wide range of real-world scenarios with minimal cost. In the following sections, we present the architecture of our method, the learning strategy informed by cross-genre knowledge, and the empirical evaluation on benchmark datasets.

Part-of-speech (POS) tagging is a core task in natural language processing, essential for a wide range of downstream applications such as syntactic parsing, information extraction, and machine translation. While substantial progress has been made in POS tagging for monolingual texts, the increasing prevalence of code-switching—specifically, the mixing of Chinese and English—presents a new and complex challenge for Chinese language processing. In modern Chinese communication, especially on the Internet and in informal written forms such as social media and emails, it is common to incorporate English terms or phrases to express new concepts or to emphasize certain ideas. Such Chinese-English mixed texts (CEMTs), often referred to as "B-language" texts, contain idiomatic and non-standard patterns that do not conform to well-established tagging frameworks. One of the major difficulties in handling these texts lies in accurately identifying and tagging the POS of the embedded English words. In the absence of a suitably annotated corpus for mixed language phenomena, many existing systems default to an oversimplified approach, marking all English words as a single, non-discriminatory category—typically labeled as "foreign words". This approach neglects the rich syntactic roles English words may play in a sentence and impacts the overall performance of linguistic analysis. In this paper, we address the issue of POS tagging in Chinese-English mixed texts by proposing a novel method that leverages dynamic features to capture contextual information more effectively than traditional, static models. Our approach introduces feature representations that evolve based on local syntactic cues and co-occurrence patterns, allowing the model to dynamically adjust its understanding of English words in the context of Chinese sentence structures. This is particularly crucial for distinguishing between function words (e.g., \textit{is}, \textit{the}) and content words (e.g., \textit{computer}, \textit{Internet}), which can behave very differently in mixed texts. We formulate this as a sequence labeling task and employ a dynamic feature-based model to capture both linguistic and contextual dependencies. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms traditional sequence labeling approaches such as Hidden Markov Models (HMHMs) and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) when applied to Chinese-English mixed text. More notably, the integration of dynamic features also leads to performance improvements in POS tagging for pure Chinese texts, indicating the general utility of our approach. Our work contributes a new perspective on handling code-switching in POS tagging, and our model offers a practical solution for improving annotation in multilingual and mixed-language environments.

The dynamic nature of social media platforms like Twitter requires continuous and real-time modeling of information to capture the evolving interests of users and the emerging trends of topics. Among various modeling approaches, topic models have been widely used for organizing, understanding, and summarizing large sets of text data. Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003) is one such probabilistic topic model that has been extensively applied in domains such as user profiling, policy monitoring, and event detection on Twitter. Traditional LDA models treat a user’s tweet history as a single document, aggregating all tweets into one to estimate user preferences over topics. However, this approach overlooks the temporal and contextual variations in short-form content, where each tweet can be considered a separate event carrying transient information (Anaby-Taviv & Dagan, 2012). To address this limitation, Twitter-LDA (Blei & Lafferty, 2009) was introduced, which assumes that each tweet is associated with a single topic, thereby improving the semantic coherence of the topics inferred for Twitter data. This approach has demonstrated superior performance over document-level LDA, especially for modeling user behavior and capturing topical distributions in social media content. Despite its advantages, Twitter-LDA is still inherently a batch-based model, restricting its utility in online or streaming environments where user interests and topic trends evolve rapidly with time. This bottleneck becomes particularly significant in contexts such as monitoring real-time public opinion, tracking breaking news, or identifying viral content. In this paper, we propose an online topic model that builds upon the foundation of Twitter-LDA but incorporates real-time inference to model the dynamics of user interests and topic trends. The contributions of this study are two-fold. First, we extend the modeling of tweets by estimating the ratio of topic-relevant words to general words per user, which allows for a more accurate representation of user behavior and diverse language use in tweets. Second, we introduce a novel method to track the evolution of topics over time by integrating the topic tracking model (TTM), originally proposed to model consumer purchase behaviors over time. By adapting TTM to the domain of social media, our model enables the online estimation of topic trends and user interest shifts, which is essential for maintaining the relevance and responsiveness of topic models in dynamic environments. This enhanced modeling approach promises to advance applications in real-time event detection, content recommendation, and social media analytics, aligning more closely with the practical demands of modern Twitter data analysis.

Abstractive summarization has emerged as a powerful alternative to extractive methods, especially for handling the complexity of news articles that span multiple documents or narratives. Its objective is to generate concise yet semantically rich summaries by paraphrasing and rephrasing the source content. A core challenge in abstractive summarization lies in the modeling of   events  —the key actions and changes that drive the content. Unlike extractive methods that select pre-existing text fragments, abstractive approaches must synthesize new sentences that adequately capture the main events and their interrelations. This necessitates a robust and flexible representation mechanism for events that abstracts away syntactic variations while preserving semantic meaning. A promising way to represent events is through   pattern clusters  , where each cluster encapsulates a distinct event (e.g., a political decision, a legal verdict), and each pattern within the cluster represents a syntactically valid way of expressing the event (e.g., "X appointed Y as the new CEO", "Y was named CEO of X"). Such representations enable a model to generate a summary that is both fluent and semantically consistent, even when the original sentences vary widely in lexical or syntactic form. In this work, we explore and compare three approaches for extracting and utilizing event patterns as part of abstractive summarization:   heuristics-based extraction  ,   compression-based extraction  , and   memory-based extraction  . Traditional abstractive systems have relied on heuristic-based methods to extract patterns, which often yield limited syntactic variety and suffer from the inability to generalize to unseen event types. Compression-based methods, which simplify input sentences before pattern extraction, offer some advantages in generalization but often sacrifice key semantic details due to over-simplification. Our main contribution lies in the proposal and successful implementation of a   memory-based approach   for pattern extraction in abstractive summarization. This method draws from a vast memory of syntactically and grammatically valid utterances, enabling the extraction of highly discriminative and informative patterns. By leveraging a database of hundreds of millions of parse trees, the memory-based method can generate patterns that are more varied, grammatically sound, and semantically precise. This, in turn, supports the generation of abstractive summaries that are not only accurate but also coherent and expressive. To manage the computational challenges of searching such a massive space of parse trees, we introduce a novel   data structure   and an efficient   search algorithm  . Our structure enables rapid identification of parse subtrees that match event expressions stored in the memory, without requiring exhaustive traversal of all existing parses.

Narrative understanding is a fundamental aspect of human cognition, enabling us to comprehend and predict sequences of events and their participants in real-world and fictional contexts. Central to this understanding is the concept of narrative schemas, which encode recurring patterns of events and their participants in structured, abstract forms. For example, a narrative schema might capture the temporal order and argument roles in a legal trial, such as arrested(POLICE, SUSPECT) followed by convicted(JUDGE, SUSPECT), where POLICE and JUDGE are semantic roles defined over lexico-syntactic patterns like "police," "agent," "authorities," or "judge" and "court." Traditionally, prior research on event structure and semantic roles has heavily relied on supervised learning, where human-annotated corpora define event classes, roles, and their properties. While these methods achieve high accuracy, they are labor-intensive, domain-bound, and not scalable to the vast and ever-evolving event patterns found in raw text. As a result, the community has shown increasing interest in unsupervised narrative modeling, which aims to extract coherent, interpretable narrative structures from unannotated text, directly from language data. In this paper, we introduce an end-to-end unsupervised framework for learning both narrative schemas and their argument roles, without relying on labeled training data, hand-generated ontologies, or task-specific constraints. Our method leverages the fact that narratives are organized around coreferent argument entities: the same person, group, or object often plays consistent roles across events in a sequence. By identifying and clustering sets of co-occurring verbs whose arguments are corefering entities, our algorithm uncovers stereotypical sequences of events—narrative schemas—that describe recurring causal and temporal relations. Unlike approaches that separately learn event structures or syntactic frames, we jointly infer both event schemas and the semantic roles of their participants, enabling richer and more robust generalization. We make three key contributions to the field of narrative modeling. First, we present a novel unsupervised learning algorithm that simultaneously infers narrative event structures and semantic roles by exploiting coreference patterns among event arguments. Second, we demonstrate the ability of our model to induce compositional, domain-agnostic event schemas and frame-specific roles, comparable to human-structured knowledge but learned solely from raw text. Third, we show that our framework improves upon existing unsupervised and semi-supervised approaches by achieving higher coherence and coverage in narrative extraction across domains. Our work opens new avenues for building language models that understand stories and scripts in a purely data-driven way, enabling applications in summarization, content planning, and question-answering in domains where structured event knowledge is absent or impractical to obtain manually.

Enabling a computer to understand a document in such a way that it can reliably answer comprehension questions presented to it is one of the most central, and yet most elusive goals of natural language processing (NLP). Such an ability is a cornerstone of higher-level language understanding tasks and constitutes the basis for many applications in question answering, automated tutoring, and information retrieval. However, the development of systems that can perform this task at human-like levels has been severely impeded by the limited availability of high-quality, annotated data. The conventional approach involving expert annotation is prohibitively expensive to scale and does not meet the demand for large datasets required by modern machine learning models. To address these issues, Hermann et al. (2015) introduced a novel reading comprehension task using the CNN and Daily Mail news datasets. By pairing news articles with their automatically generated bullet-point summaries, the authors created a massive, annotated dataset comprising over a million training examples. They demonstrated that a neural network model can achieve strong performance on this task, opening up new possibilities for research in reading comprehension and text understanding. In this paper, we present a comprehensive and systematic examination of this newly established reading comprehension task. Our aim is to understand the depth of linguistic and contextual understanding that is necessary to perform well on this benchmark and to assess its utility as a proxy for general reading comprehension capability. We take a dual approach toward this goal. First, we perform a qualitative, hand-based analysis of a carefully selected subset of examples from the CNN and Daily Mail datasets. This analysis allows us to explore the types of reasoning and inference the task requires, such as fact identification, paraphrase recognition, and implicit information retrieval. Second, we develop and evaluate a set of simple, yet carefully engineered baseline systems that rely on minimal linguistic knowledge and crude heuristics. These models achieve notable performance metrics—72.4% accuracy on the CNN dataset and 75.8% accuracy on the Daily Mail dataset—surpassing the current state-of-the-art by over 5% in both cases. These results indicate that high performance on this task does not necessarily require sophisticated neural architectures or deep language understanding, thereby raising important questions about the task's capacity to evaluate true reading comprehension ability. Given these findings, we analyze what may constitute the upper bound of performance on this dataset based on various heuristics and constraints of the problem structure.

In the era of big data, user-generated text content, such as comments and reviews on online platforms, has become an invaluable source of information for understanding user preferences and item characteristics. In particular, text comments provide rich, nuanced insights that numerical ratings often fail to capture. Recommendation systems, which are critical in modern e-commerce and content discovery platforms, have traditionally relied on passive user-item rating data for generating personalized recommendations. However, this approach has multiple limitations—it often suffers from sparsity, ignores the semantic context behind user preferences, and is prone to overgeneralization or underfitting when user and item feature spaces are not well characterized. The integration of textual data into recommendation systems thus presents a promising direction to enhance prediction accuracy and explainability. Traditional collaborative filtering techniques and their matrix completion variants focus primarily on uncovering latent factors based on co-occurrence of user-item interactions. While effective in some scenarios, these methods do not exploit the rich contextual information in user-generated text. On the other hand, opinion mining and sentiment analysis tools are frequently designed for tasks like emotional polarity classification, aspect-based sentiment analysis, or topic modeling. Although these methods extract valuable insights from text, they often output abstract, often unstructured information that is not directly actionable in recommendation tasks. What is missing is a unified framework that can simultaneously learn interpretable, generalizable, and task-specific distributed representations from text reviews, which can then be integrated into a standard recommendation pipeline. In this paper, we address these limitations by proposing an approach to learn distributed representations for users and items from text reviews toward the goal of enhancing recommendation systems. Our approach leverages the full-text content of reviews to construct compact vector representations of user and item profiles. These representations are learned under a unified framework in which the primary objective is to maximize the likelihood of observing word appearances in the textual context about user-item interactions. This setup ensures that the learned vectors capture not only the explicit semantic information in the text but also the underlying user-item relationships that are relevant to the recommendation task. A critical innovation in our work is the development of a recommendation-aware distributed representation approach. By aligning the learning objective of the model with the downstream recommendation task, we enable accurate prediction of user-item interaction scores on previously unseen pairs, even in the absence of textual data.

This paper introduces a probabilistic model for the resolution of associative anaphora in Japanese. Associative anaphora, a subtype of bridging anaphora, is unique in that the anaphor and its antecedent are not coreferent. Instead, they are connected based on semantic or contextual associations. Resolving such references is a challenging task in natural language processing, as it requires understanding the implicit relationships between expressions without explicit pronouns or markers. A complicating factor is the frequent use of zero anaphora in Japanese, where antecedents are omitted and must be inferred from the discourse. Our proposed model addresses the problem by treating associative anaphora as a variant of zero anaphora. This allows us to leverage established methods for zero anaphora resolution and integrate them into a unified probabilistic framework. The model employs automatically acquired lexical knowledge to establish associations between potential antecedents and anaphoric expressions. By making use of prior linguistic and contextual information, we enhance the system's ability to disambiguate and select the most probable antecedent for an associative anaphor. A key component of the model is the joint resolution of associative and zero anaphora within the same inference framework. This approach avoids the problem of sequential errors and leverages the contextual interdependencies between these two types of anaphora. Experimental evaluation on a standard Japanese corpus demonstrates that the model achieves strong performance in resolving associative anaphora. Furthermore, results show a significant improvement in accuracy when associative and zero anaphora are resolved simultaneously, compared to isolated resolution of each type. These findings highlight the benefits of an integrated and probabilistic approach to anaphora resolution in language with a high degree of zero pronoun usage. Overall, the model provides an effective way to handle associative anaphora in Japanese and offers a promising direction for improving anaphora resolution in other morphologically rich languages with similar phenomena. This work contributes not only to the advancement of Japanese NLP but also to the broader understanding of bridging anaphora and the development of robust, language-independent computational models for discourse analysis.
