This work is supported by the MEXT Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research (B). Understanding the mechanisms behind associative anaphora is crucial for tasks such as machine translation, question answering, and discourse modeling, particularly in languages like Japanese where such references are common but structurally implicit.

The automated induction of semantic taxonomies is a foundational task in natural language processing, with significant implications for knowledge representation, information retrieval, and question answering. Traditional methods often rely on curated linguistic resources such as WordNet, which require extensive manual curation and are thus limited in coverage and extensibility to domain-specific vocabularies or emerging concepts. The task of taxonomy induction seeks to address this issue by automatically discovering hierarchical relationships—most notably, hypernymy (is-a) relationships—among entities in a given domain, leveraging unstructured or weakly structured data as input. While significant progress has been made in this area, the challenge of integrating diverse types of relational evidence into a coherent and scalable system remains open. In this paper, we present a novel structured learning approach for taxonomy induction that models the problem using probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) and benefits from the joint modeling of hypernym and sibling relationships. The extracted structure is informed by a rich set of features derived from Web n-gram statistics and Wikipedia abstracts, capturing both statistical and semantic patterns across a vast corpus of textual data. Our key insight is to treat the taxonomy as a structured output directly, thereby relaxing the assumption that individual relations (such as hypernymy or siblinghood) can be learned independently and scored in isolation. To enable efficient learning and inference over complex, potentially cyclical structures, we employ loopy belief propagation (LBP), a message-passing algorithm known for its effectiveness in approximate inference on undirected graphical models. In addition, we incorporate a directed spanning tree algorithm to efficiently model the core hypernymy factor in the taxonomy, ensuring tractable computation even for large-scale datasets. This hybrid approach allows us to manage the inherent complexity of hierarchical relationships while preserving the flexibility and robustness required for noisy, real-world data. To train our model, we adopt a discriminative setup using a subgraph of WordNet as supervision. Instead of learning from individual hypernym labels, we use adaptive subgradient stochastic optimization (e.g., AdaGrad) to train over local sub-structures extracted from the existing taxonomy, enabling our system to learn to replicate accurate hierarchies from example data. This discriminative learning is augmented by our ability to incorporate heterogeneous relational signals, such as evidence of sibling relationships which, as our experiments demonstrate, contribute significantly to overall performance. Empirically, our approach achieves a 51% reduction in error over a chance baseline in reconstructing sub-hierarchies of WordNet.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable success in recent years, primarily through deep architectures that model the translation process in an end-to-end fashion. A key component of these models is the attention mechanism, which allows the decoder to focus selectively on different parts of the source sentence during translation, thereby improving fluency and context awareness. However, NMT systems designed for purely textual tasks often fail to incorporate additional contextual modalities—such as visual information—into the translation process. In many real-world applications, such as image captioning into a foreign language or translating text in visual contexts (e.g., navigation signs or advertisements), the image provides critical additional information that aids disambiguation and enhances translation quality. The integration of visual features into NMT presents both an opportunity and a challenge. On one hand, visual context can help resolve ambiguity by indicating the real-world situation or object referred to in the source text. On the other hand, it is not straightforward to model and integrate global visual features into the deep neural structures of a translation system while preserving the core advantages of existing text-based NMT models. In this paper, we present a novel approach that incorporates global image features into the components of an attention-based neural machine translation pipeline in a systematic and extensible manner. We extract global visual features using a pre-trained convolutional neural network and incorporate them into the NMT model in three distinct but complementary ways: (i) as pseudo-words in the source sentence, (ii) by initializing the encoder hidden state with visual features, and (iii) as additional inputs to initialize the decoder hidden state. Our method ensures that the visual features influence both the encoding of the source sentence and the decoding process for the target language. We experiment with these strategies in two language settings: English and German, using the popular Multi30k dataset, which provides aligned image-text corpora. In addition to comparing different architectures for visual incorporation, we investigate the impact of adding synthetic multi-modal, multilingual training data. Our results demonstrate that multi-modal models trained with visual features consistently outperform their purely text-based counterparts. Specifically, our best-performing model achieves state-of-the-art results on the Multi30k dataset. Significantly, and to our knowledge for the first time, a purely neural NMT model outperforms a strong Phrase-Based Statistical Machine Translation (PBSMT) model by a considerable margin according to all metrics evaluated (e.g., BLEU, METEOR, and TER).

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have demonstrated the effectiveness of unsupervised pre-trained word embeddings in capturing linguistic patterns and semantic relationships from large quantities of unlabeled text (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014; Peters et al., 2018). These embeddings often serve as either initializations or fixed components in supervised task-specific models, where they guide the learning process by providing contextualized semantic representations. However, conventional modeling approaches typically separate the unsupervised feature extraction and supervised task learning phases. In this work, we propose a method that integrates task-specific and language-general feature learning within a single training pipeline. Specifically, we extend the loss function of a classification model by incorporating an unsupervised objective at the word-embedding level, encouraging the model to refine its representations to be both task-informative and linguistically rich. This dual learning objective is particularly useful for domains where task-specific data is limited and where incorporating general linguistic knowledge can be crucial for performance, such as temporal relation classification. Temporal relation classification is a key aspect of temporal information extraction tasks, which aim to determine the temporal ordering of events in text. One important subtype of temporal relations is narrative containment, which identifies whether one event temporally contains another within a narrative sequence (e.g., a task encompassing subtasks or a procedure with multiple stages). Accurate temporal relation extraction is essential for applications such as medical information extraction, where reasoning about event sequences can have significant diagnostic or therapeutic implications (Mohnannis et al., 2014; Uzuner et al., 2011). In this paper, we focus specifically on the narrative containment relation and apply our method to the Temporal History of Present Illness in Medical Evaluations (THYME) dataset (Chu et al., 2012), a benchmark for temporal reasoning in clinical text. The key insight of our approach is to tie the refinement of task-specific feature representations to the underlying structure of the language itself. While traditional word embeddings capture general language patterns, they often lack task-specific properties that could improve temporal reasoning. By contrasting our auxiliary loss with the primary classification loss, we aim to push word representations to co-adapt to both the static syntactic clues (e.g., part-of-speech, grammatical roles) and the dynamic context of temporal relations. In doing so, we align our model with domain-specific features while preserving the linguistic quality of the embeddings. We evaluate our method by comparing it to a standard fine-tuning setup as well as models with combined loss components, where the auxiliary objectives are applied at higher-level representations.

Sentence Similarity (SS) is a fundamental task in natural language processing that focuses on calculating a similarity score between two sentences. The SS task stands out from higher-level semantic tasks, such as document-level classification or clustering, due to the limited lexical diversity within a sentence. Sentences, as the basic unit in SS, typically contain a smaller set of words and instances, often resulting in sparsity and underrepresentation of contextual cues. This sparsity makes the accurate modeling of individual words critical for capturing the intended semantic meaning of a sentence. In particular, understanding lexical semantics—especially richer and more nuanced aspects like selectional preferences and word similarity—can significantly enhance the performance of SS systems. Lexical semantics is the study of meaning at the level of words and how they combine in sentences. Selectional preferences, for example, refer to the constraints a word imposes on the words it co-occurs with, and they provide crucial clues for understanding how words function in context. For instance, the verb "eat" tends to co-occur with animate agents like "person" or "animal," but not with inanimate objects. Similarly, the notion of lexical similarity, which includes synonyms and near-synonyms, contributes to capturing the impacts of word substitution and paraphrasing in sentences. These aspects of lexical semantics, however, are often overlooked or considered secondary in traditional sentence modeling approaches. In this paper, we argue that robust modeling of lexical semantics can improve the representation of sentential semantics. To this end, we propose a latent variable model that incorporates both corpus-based and knowledge-based lexical information. Specifically, we integrate selectional preferences derived from co-occurrence patterns in a large corpus and similar words extracted from linguistic resources such as dictionaries. These sources are encoded into a unified latent structure that enables the model to capture how lexical choices affect sentence meaning. By leveraging both data-driven and language-driven knowledge, the model becomes more robust in handling rare and unseen word combinations that are common in the SS task. We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed model. Our results show that the latent variable model achieves state-of-the-art performance among unsupervised SS systems on two widely used benchmark datasets. Notably, the performance gains are attributed to the incorporation of lexical semantic properties, which allow the model to better distinguish between semantically related and unrelated sentences. This work represents a meaningful step toward building sentence similarity models that not only learn from data but also benefit from well-curated lexical knowledge.

Medical Event Detection (MED) from unstructured text in Electronic Health Records (EHRs) plays a critical role in advancing semantic understanding and enabling data-driven decision-making in healthcare. EHRs contain rich narratives, such as clinical notes, progress reports, and discharge summaries, which are key sources of information for identifying medical events, including diagnoses, treatments, and adverse drug reactions. The accurate extraction and classification of these events are essential for supporting applications such as pharmacovigilance, drug surveillance, and cohort identification for clinical trials. Traditional approaches to MED typically rely on feature engineering and sequence labeling models like Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), which utilize domain-specific rules and features derived from fixed context windows. While these methods have achieved moderate success, they often struggle to capture the dynamic and context-dependent nature of medical language, leading to suboptimal performance when dealing with the complexity and ambiguity present in clinical text. Deep learning has emerged as a promising alternative in sequence modeling tasks due to its capacity to automatically learn contextualized representations from raw data. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), in particular, have demonstrated strong capabilities for modeling sequential dependencies, which is especially relevant in the context of MED, where the meaning of a term can be influenced by its surrounding tokens. In this work, we investigate the application of Bidirectional RNNs (BiRNNs) for medical event detection in EHRs. Unlike unidirectional RNNs, which process input sequences in a single temporal direction, BiRNNs combine forward and backward hidden layers to capture both past and future context, making them well-suited for labeling sequences in NLP tasks. Our results show that the BiRNN model significantly outperforms traditional CRF-based approaches in detecting medical events and their associated attributes across a benchmark EHR dataset. We further explore how leveraging rich contextual embeddings and the inherent sequential structure of the data contributes to improved model accuracy and generalizability. Our findings highlight the potential of deep learning techniques, particularly BiRNNs, in revolutionizing the current state of the art for medical information extraction tasks. By demonstrating the superior performance of RNNs over conventional models, this study provides a strong foundation for future research into end-to-end deep learning approaches for semantic processing of EHR data. The broader implications of this work lie in its potential to facilitate the transformation of unstructured clinical narratives into structured information, thereby enabling the realization of precision medicine and data-driven healthcare analytics. Entity linking (EL) is a core task in natural language processing, where the goal is to disambiguate mentions of entities—such as "Apple"—in text and link them to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base (KB) like Wikipedia or Wikidata. Accurate entity linking is essential for downstream tasks like information retrieval, question answering, and knowledge graph construction. Despite recent advances, entity linking remains challenging due to the ambiguity of natural language and the variability of contexts across different documents and domains. A robust EL system must be capable of capturing diverse aspects of an entity and its mention, including the entity's description in the KB, the linguistic context in which it appears, and its semantic type. Traditional EL methods often rely on hand-crafted features such as entity surface forms, token co-occurrence statistics, or manually annotated entity types. However, these approaches require domain-specific adaptation and can be brittle when applied to unseen domains. Neural network-based approaches have shown promise in better capturing the complex patterns required for EL, particularly when using representations learned in an end-to-end manner from large text corpora. Nevertheless, many existing models treat the various sources of entity information—such as type, description, and context—in isolation, failing to exploit the potential synergies that their joint encoding might offer. Moreover, as knowledge bases are often static and incomplete, any EL system must also be able to link mentions of newly emerging entities that are not yet present in the KB. In this work, we introduce a novel neural, modular entity linking system that learns a unified dense representation for each entity by integrating multiple heterogeneous sources of information. Our approach simultaneously encodes an entity's structured types, its KB description, and the linguistic context surrounding each mention. This joint encoding allows the model to better capture the semantic nuance of an entity and disambiguate mentions more effectively. Our model is designed to be modular, allowing for efficient training and generalization across different domains without the need for domain-specific training data or hand-engineered features. We evaluate our system on benchmark datasets across multiple domains and demonstrate that it achieves competitive performance, at times outperforming state-of-the-art EL systems. Additionally, we show that our approach is effective at handling out-of-KB entities, providing accurate linkage for mentioned entities that do not yet have an entry in the knowledge base.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable success in recent years, primarily through end-to-end architectures that learn to map sequences of words from a source language to a target language. Despite these advances, standard NMT models are typically trained to translate sentences in isolation and often fail to incorporate higher-level contextual information that can be crucial for disambiguating lexical ambiguity, preserving consistent terminology, and modeling discourse-level relationships. This is particularly important for translating documents that span multiple sentences or paragraphs, where maintaining coherence and fluency across longer stretches of text is essential for human readability and system performance. Recent research has demonstrated that leveraging context can significantly enhance translation quality by providing a more comprehensive representation of the input (Costa-jussà and Fonollosa, 2016; Sennrich et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2017). In this paper, we present a novel approach to document-level NMT by incorporating a hierarchical attention mechanism that captures contextual information in a structured and dynamic manner. Our model extends the conventional sentence-based NMT architecture by adding a new hierarchical component that conditions on the NMT model's own previous hidden states, thereby enabling the system to maintain and utilize a short-term memory of previous translations within the same document. Specifically, the hierarchical attention mechanism introduces two levels of attention: one for modeling the internal structure of the current sentence and another for dynamically aggregating contextual information from surrounding sentences. This dual-level structure allows the model to selectively attend to both the local sentence context and the broader document context as needed, facilitating better coherence in translation. The document-level context is encoded using a second-level recurrent neural network (RNN) that processes the encoder hidden states of previously translated sentences. This hierarchical setup allows the decoder to make translation decisions not only based on the current sentence but also informed by the global structure of the document. We evaluate our model on a range of document-level translation tasks using data from publicly available and industry-standard datasets, including both parallel and monolingual documents. Our results show that the hierarchical attention model consistently outperforms strong baseline NMT systems, achieving an improvement of 0.45 BLEU points over existing state-of-the-art methods in context-aware translation. Furthermore, we observe that both the encoder and decoder benefit from the integration of document context, with the encoder capturing contextual dependencies during source sentence encoding and the decoder incorporating this information in the generation process to enhance fluency and coherence.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have increasingly focused on opinion and sentiment analysis, especially in identifying how opinions are directed toward specific entities and events. A particularly nuanced and underexplored area involves  +/-effect events —events described as having positive or negative consequences for certain entities—toward which opinions are often implicitly or explicitly expressed. For instance, the event “pass an exam” is typically perceived as beneficial to the student, a +effect event, whereas “lose a job” is a -effect event involving negative consequences for the employee. Understanding the polarity of such events is essential for opinion inference, where the goal is to model how different agents evaluate prior occurrences in discourse. A critical enabler for such inference is the availability of a rich, reliable lexicon of event types annotated with their +/-effect properties. Existing lexicons, however, are often limited in either coverage, granularity, or in their ability to handle the complex semantic structure of event expressions. Many words can refer to multiple events depending on their context, a phenomenon known as  sense ambiguity . For example, the verb  earn  might refer to a +effect event like  earning a promotion  or a -effect event like  earning a reprimand , depending on the context. Therefore, a sense-level, rather than word-level, approach is necessary to capture the precise semantics of event expressions. This paper presents –/+EffectWordNet, a novel resource for sense-level identification of +/-effect events. Drawing on the structured semantic network of WordNet, we implement a graph-based algorithm that propagates sense-level effect annotations through semantic relations. This is complemented by a classifier that utilizes sense dictionary (gloss) information to predict +/-effect properties. By combining the structural and lexical knowledge components, we propose a hybrid model that outperforms both individual approaches. We demonstrate not only the accuracy of the model but also its effectiveness in augmenting manual annotation efforts. Our results indicate that the model can successfully identify +/–effect senses that do not appear in the initial seed set, thereby improving the scalability and precision of lexicon construction for opinion inference. Sentence compression is a key technique in natural language processing (NLP) used for text simplification, summarization, and information extraction. It aims to shorten a given sentence while preserving its core meaning and factual content, often by removing non-essential information such as redundant phrases or syntactic filler words. Traditionally, sentence compression has been studied and implemented in a monolingual context, with models trained and evaluated on data from a single language. This monolingual approach has led to significant advances in creating compact, readable sentence variants tailored to specific linguistic patterns and syntactic structures. However, the monolingual perspective limits the application of sentence compression in multilingual settings, where content is simultaneously available in multiple languages and processed across language boundaries. With the increasing demand for multilingual NLP tools and the growth of cross-lingual technologies such as machine translation, cross-lingual retrieval, and multilingual summarization, there is a need to extend sentence compression to a bilingual context. This paper proposes Parallel Sentence Compression, a novel formulation of the sentence compression task in which the goal is to generate compressed, parallel sentence pairs from a given set of aligned, full-length sentences in two languages. By ensuring that both compressed sentences are not only shorter versions of their longer counterparts but also maintain high alignment with each other, parallel compression can significantly benefit downstream multilingual tasks by reducing data size without sacrificing utility. For example, in multilingual summarization, parallel compression could help maintain structural and semantic coherence across language pairs while reducing redundancy and computational requirements. We investigate two distinct strategies for incorporating bilingual information into the compression process: (1) a source language–first approach where compression is applied in the source language and then the compressed version is translated to the target language, and (2) a joint compression method where both sentences in the parallel pair are compressed simultaneously using shared knowledge from the bilingual context. Our experiments are conducted on a parallel news corpus, allowing for systematic evaluation of both methods under controlled and realistic settings. The evaluation focuses on compression quality, parallel alignment fidelity, and the ability of the compressed sentences to retain semantic consistency across languages. The motivation for this work is twofold: First, it addresses a practical need in multilingual NLP pipelines to handle compressed and parallel text as compact input representations. Second, it opens a new research direction by exploring how multilingual signals can be integrated into sentence compression, with the potential to improve alignment-based models and reduce cross-lingual information asymmetry.

Chinese syntactic analysis is a foundational task in natural language processing, encompassing several subtasks such as word segmentation, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and dependency parsing. In traditional systems, these tasks are often modeled as cascading pipelines, where the output of one task (e.g., word segmentation) is used as input for the next (e.g., POS tagging). While this modular approach has driven significant progress in Chinese NLP, a major limitation is the error propagation problem: errors from early tasks can compound and significantly affect the performance of later downstream tasks. To address this, joint modeling approaches have been proposed that integrate the tasks within a unified framework, allowing the model to exploit correlations among the subtasks and reduce error propagation. Recent advances in deep learning have brought remarkable improvements to NLP tasks, especially in syntactic analysis. However, the vast majority of neural-based approaches for Chinese syntactic analysis have focused on individual tasks or transition-based systems that assume pre-segmented input, often using word embeddings to capture linguistic context. While word embeddings are effective, they rely on prior knowledge of word boundaries, which is not compatible with a fully joint architecture that requires simultaneous output of both word segmentation and syntactic structures. This restricts the applicability of previous neural models to early-stage Chinese processing tasks such as joint modeling. This paper introduces a neural joint model for Chinese syntactic analysis that simultaneously performs word segmentation, POS tagging, and dependency parsing in a transition-based framework. To overcome the limitations of word embeddings in the joint task setting, we propose the use of character string embeddings, which are applied at the character level and can also capture phrasal patterns. This enables our model to learn contextual representations without assuming prior segmentation, making it suitable for the fully joint processing of Chinese text. Our key contributions are as follows: (1) We develop a neural transition-based joint model that performs word segmentation, POS tagging, and dependency parsing as a unified task, avoiding error propagation and leveraging inter-task correlations; (2) We introduce character string embeddings that complement traditional word embeddings in the joint task setting, demonstrating their effectiveness in capturing minimal linguistic units and improving overall coherence; (3) We conduct extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, showing that our model outperforms existing systems in word segmentation and POS tagging, while achieving competitive or superior performance in dependency parsing. Furthermore, we explore a simplified version of our model using bi-directional long short-term memory (bi-LSTM) networks with fewer features, demonstrating that high performance can be retained even with a reduced feature set.

Ontologies play a critical role in representing structured knowledge in a domain-specific context, organizing entities and the relationships between them in a formal and semantically meaningful way. They serve as the backbone for various applications, including knowledge base construction, semantic search, and intelligent systems. However, as the development of ontologies is often carried out independently by different communities or organizations dealing with the same domain, this leads to   parallel ontologies  —ontologies that share a common domain but differ in structure, nomenclature, or details. In such cases,   ontology matching   is a necessary process to align semantically equivalent or related entities across ontologies. This alignment not only reduces redundancy but also enhances interoperability and reusability of knowledge. Ontology matching has typically relied on heuristic-based similarity measures, such as lexical, structural, and semantic alignment techniques. However, traditional methods often struggle with scalability, domain dependence, and the lack of sufficient training data, especially for rare or ambiguous terms. With the advent of   deep learning   and continuous word representations (i.e.,   word embeddings  ), there has been a growing interest in leveraging   representation learning   to capture semantic relationships directly from text or structured data. Despite the progress, most current methods for ontology matching still face two key limitations: (1) reliance on manually curated training data or domain-specific features, and (2) the use of general-purpose word embeddings that may not reflect the   specific semantic needs of ontological entities  . This paper addresses these limitations by introducing   DeepAlignment  , a novel and   completely unsupervised   entity alignment framework for ontology matching. DeepAlignment is designed to refine   pre-trained word vectors   using ontology-specific information to derive meaningful and domain-adapted representations of ontological entities. Unlike supervised approaches that require labeled alignment pairs or task-specific features, DeepAlignment operates in an   unsupervised learning   regime, where the refining process is driven by the structure and semantics of the ontologies themselves. This is achieved by iteratively adjusting the embeddings using a   refinement objective   that captures the relational patterns inherent in the ontologies, leading to more accurate and semantically coherent entity representations. Our framework is centered on the idea that   ontology entities are better aligned when their embeddings reflect both their individual semantics and their relationships to other entities in the ontology  . To this end, DeepAlignment incorporates a learning strategy that accounts for the hierarchical and relational structure of the ontologies, enabling improvements in alignment accuracy even without human supervision. We evaluate DeepAlignment on standard ontology matching benchmarks, including widely used datasets from the   Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative (OAEI)  .

Medical coding is a critical aspect of healthcare systems, underpinning billing, treatment tracking, and epidemiological research. Clinical notes, typewritten narratives documenting patient encounters, often contain detailed yet unstructured descriptions of symptoms, diagnoses, and interventions. These notes are typically annotated with standardized medical codes, such as ICD-9 or ICD-10 for diagnoses, and CPT for procedures, providing a formal representation of the clinical information they contain. The manual transcription and coding of clinical notes is a painstaking process, both time-consuming and costly, while also being susceptible to human error. Moreover, the absence of explicit explanations linking the codified diagnoses and treatments to the textual content makes it difficult for clinicians and researchers to understand the reasoning and justifications behind specific coding decisions. The intersection of natural language processing (NLP) and clinical informatics has seen growing interest in the automation of medical code prediction from unstructured text. A key challenge in this area is not only achieving high predictive accuracy, but also ensuring that the system provides  interpretable  explanations for its decisions, especially in a high-stakes domain like medicine where transparency is paramount. While early approaches focused on keyword matching and rule-based systems—methods that can produce brittle and insufficiently accurate results—modern approaches have moved toward leveraging deep learning, particularly neural architectures that can capture complex, context-dependent patterns in clinical language. In this paper, we present an attentional convolutional neural network (CNN) for predicting medical codes from clinical text. The proposed architecture combines the strong pattern-discovery capabilities of CNNs with an explicit attention mechanism, which allows the model to not only identify relevant information in the text but also highlight the justifications for each prediction. Segment-based attention is employed to dynamically weigh and aggregate the most relevant portions of the document for each potential code, enabling the model to handle the vast output space (typically thousands of possible codes) while maintaining interpretability. Our evaluations show that the system is both accurate and explainable. In predictive performance, the model outperforms existing methods for multi-label classification of medical codes, achieving a precision@8 of 0.71 and a Micro-F1 score of 0.54 on standard benchmark datasets. We further evaluate the  interpretability  of the system by presenting attention-derived segments to a practicing physician and asking them to assess the relevance and meaningfulness of those explanations for each code assignment. The physician's feedback confirms that the attention mechanism successfully identifies text segments that are clinically meaningful and informative, validating the model's utility not only as a prediction tool but also as a decision-support aid that enhances transparency and trust in the clinical workflow.

Voice search has become a vital interface for users seeking information on mobile devices, especially in the context of local business directory assistance. The rise of smartphones and smart speakers has fueled the demand for more natural and convenient ways to access local services, from finding the nearest restaurant to making a reservation over the phone using voice queries. Despite the convenience, however, current speech recognition systems face significant challenges in accurately processing spoken queries for local businesses. This is particularly acute for business listing names, which often include niche or unique titles and may not be well represented in standard language models. When users mispronounce or are misunderstood, the result is low accuracy, poor user experience, and ultimately, reduced trust in the system. Traditional speech recognition systems rely on static language models, often trained on vast amounts of general text data, such as news articles or web content. However, these models are not optimized for the specific vocabulary and context of local business directories. As a result, speech recognition engines often fail to interpret queries correctly, leading to high error rates and user frustration. The limitations are exacerbated in regions with non-standard dialects, accents, or local business naming conventions that deviate from common language usage. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to enhance speech recognition accuracy for local business voice search by introducing  geo-centric language models . Our algorithm is specifically designed for the domain of business directory assistance services and addresses the shortcomings of conventional language models by dynamically adapting to the geographic and lexical characteristics of local business data. The key idea is to generate language models that are centered around the user's location, capturing the unique vocabulary and nomenclature of businesses in the area. By doing so, we are able to significantly improve recognition accuracy while also optimizing for real-time performance. Our geo-centric language model is built using a combination of user location, business directory data, and statistical modeling techniques. Given the user's geographic area, we extract relevant business names and other related terms and use them to construct a compact and focused language model. This model not only reflects the local business landscape but is also optimized for fast recognition due to its smaller, curated vocabulary. Importantly, it is pre-compiled, enabling rapid deployment and consistent performance across a wide range of devices and platforms. We evaluate our geo-centric language models using real-world spoken business listing name queries collected from a large-scale business directory assistance service.

Numbers like "131 million dollars" can often feel abstract and difficult to grasp. A dollar sign and a large number string like 131,000,000 convey factual magnitude, but without contextual framing, they yield little intuitive meaning to lay readers. For example, such a number can represent a corporate revenue, a government funding allocation, or the cost of an infrastructure project—but without deeper context, all readers see is a high value with no perceptible scale. Such context is critical for interpretable communication, particularly in news media where numbers often dominate factual reporting. To aid in this interpretability challenge, we introduce a new task: quantifying numerical mentions in text by  compositional perspective generation . The goal of this task is to produce  perspective descriptions  that anchor abstract numbers to familiar or relatable quantities. For instance, the number "131 million" might be turned into a sentence such as,  "$131 million is about the cost to employ everyone in Texas over a lunch period"  — a description that moves from an abstract figure to a concrete scenario. This form of contextual elaboration directly addresses the human need for qualitative benchmarking of quantities and can be particularly valuable in filtering misinformation, clarifying news statements, and bridging comprehension gaps across demographics. To support this novel task, we first create a dataset by collecting numeric mentions from news articles and manually labeling them with a set of rated perspective candidates. These examples form a rich set of domain-agnostic anchors that can be used to ground numerical values in real-world experiences, geographic references, or social contexts. We then present a system designed to generate perspectives algorithmically, operating in two stages:  formula construction  and  description generation . In the first stage, we compose  formulae  using numeric facts from a structured knowledge base. Given the gold standard of such formulae, we explore how they can be ranked and filtered based on factors such as familiarity, numeric proximity, and semantic compatibility. The second stage,  description generation , translates the selected formulae into natural language using a sequence-to-sequence recurrent neural network model. This model generalizes across diverse inputs and maintains fluency and coherence while capturing the essence of the numerical context. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this compositional approach. At the formula construction stage, our model achieves a 15.2% improvement in F1 score over a non-compositional baseline, and our description generation model attains a 12.5 BLEU point improvement over a strong baseline.

Recent advances in distributional semantics have focused on capturing the multiple meanings (senses) of polysemous words in vector space models. Traditional approaches to word representation often struggle with polysemy, as they produce a single fixed vector per word, conflating all possible senses into a single representation. To address this, multi-sense models aim to learn separate embeddings for different word senses while leveraging the structure of context to disambiguate them. Most prior work has relied solely on monolingual corpora and has not incorporated cross-lingual information, which is particularly under-explored in the context of discrete multi-sense representations. In this paper, we introduce a bilingual approach to multi-sense embedding learning that leverages both monolingual and cross-lingual signals to improve the quality of learned word representations. Our model is centered around a discrete autoencoder framework, where the encoder selects a sense for a target word by attending to both monolingual and bilingual contextual information—especially, parallel sentences between two languages—which are frequently aligned in machine translation and cross-lingual tasks. The decoder, given the selected sense, then reconstructs the lexical context in which the word appeared, using a sense-aware transformation of the encoded information. Importantly, the encoder and decoder components are jointly estimated, enabling the model to learn a shared, structured representation space where both senses and contexts are effectively aligned across languages. One of the key contributions of our approach is the use of discrete latent variables to represent word senses, as opposed to the continuous latent space commonly employed in VAE-based models. Discrete sense variables allow for more interpretable and modular sense representations, which are better suited to tasks that require sense disambiguation or cross-lingual alignment. Moreover, through the use of parallel data, our model exploits the implicit semantic correspondences between source and target languages to enhance the learning of sense-rich representations. Notably, we find that even though cross-lingual information is not used during evaluation, the representations induced from bilingual data consistently outperform their monolingual counterparts across a suite of tasks that require capturing multiple word senses. This suggests that integrating bilingual context provides a strong inductive bias for the model, helping it to discover more accurate and coherent sense distinctions. Our experimental results are evaluated on standard tasks such as English to French word similarity and cross-lingual word sense disambiguation. In the context of multi-sense representation learning, our work contributes a new method for building discrete, bilingual word embeddings, demonstrating that cross-lingual data can be a powerful resource for capturing fine-grained semantic distinctions in polysemous words.

Linguistic alignment is a pervasive phenomenon in human conversation, referring to the tendency of interlocutors to adopt similar linguistic forms when communicating with each other. This alignment can manifest in various ways, such as syntactic structure, phonetic realization, or lexical choice, and has been shown to play a crucial role in facilitating communication, maintaining conversational coherence, and fostering social rapport. Theoretical models suggest that linguistic alignment arises from cognitive mechanisms like memory retrieval or similarity-based processing (Brown and Gygax, 2003), and it has been extensively studied in experimental and observational settings (Pickering and Garrod, 2004; Barr et al., 2010). In recent years, researchers have also explored the influence of social factors on alignment, particularly the role of social power—a construct commonly associated with status, authority, or influence in interpersonal interactions. Driven by the intuition that power imbalances might shape how dialogue participants influence each other linguistically, previous studies have often reported that individuals in positions of higher power tend to "anchor" the interaction and receive more alignment, whereas their lower-power interlocutors show greater variability in their linguistic choices (Barr et al., 2010; Farhadi et al., 2020). For instance, such findings have been interpreted as evidence that power dynamics rhythmically modulate conversational influence, with the powerholder exerting a stabilizing and/or directive force on the linguistic trajectory of the interaction. While these insights have offered a compelling narrative of power in language, they also raise critical questions about the mechanisms underpinning the observed patterns—particularly given the richness of the linguistic and social variables present in natural dialogue. One area that remains underexplored in this literature is the role of low-level linguistic features, such as utterance length, syntactic complexity, or verbal clarity, in shaping alignment patterns. These features can be highly informative correlates of linguistic influence that are often conflated with social power. For example, if individuals with higher social power tend to produce longer or more complex utterances (possibly due to conversational dominance), it is possible that such alignment preferences are not driven by power per se, but rather by these superficially observable attributes. This paper investigates the relationship between social power and linguistic alignment using two independently collected observational dialog datasets, each annotated for speaker-specific social power attributes. Our goal is twofold: (1) to assess the extent to which social power predicts linguistic alignment in dialogue, and (2) to assess whether this relationship persists when accounting for low-level linguistic features.

Parsing and recovering dependencies between predicates and their arguments is a fundamental requirement for semantic interpretation in natural language processing. Dependency structures, especially unbounded dependencies such as long-distance extraction or gap-filling constructions (e.g., wh-questions, pied-piping, or movement phenomena), often pose significant challenges for standard dependency parsers due to the ambiguity and syntactic complexity they introduce. Accurately identifying these unbounded dependencies is critical for tasks involving semantic role labeling, information extraction, and question answering, where the semantic roles and long-distance interactions are essential for correct interpretation. Traditional syntactic frameworks have attempted to address the problem of unbounded dependencies through formal specifications of grammatical constraints. For example, Head-Driven Phrase Structure Grammar (HPSG) and the Penn Treebank encodings based on Government and Binding Theory (GB) capture a detailed syntactic structure, yet they often require large numbers of complex grammatical categories and rules to encode the relationships between constituents. These systems are often difficult to scale and insufficiently robust for tasks requiring semantic composition. Categorial grammars, on the other hand, offer a more uniform and elegant approach by modeling syntax and semantics through lexical functions that directly encode combination operations, often using a small and consistent set of rules based on functor-argument structure. This paper introduces a novel formalization of categorial grammar that combines the advantages of categorial composition with the grammatical generalization found in HPSG-based systems. Specifically, our grammar is  generalized  in that it reduces the number of syntactic categories to only those necessary to enforce grammatical constraints while preserving the expressive power required for unbounded dependencies. By doing so, the grammar becomes more tractable for parsing and learning while maintaining the ability to capture complex syntactic and semantic relations accurately. A central contribution of this work is the development of a novel reannotation system that maps existing linguistic resources such as the Penn Treebank—based on GB-style representations—into the proposed categorial grammar. This system allows us to leverage the extensive manual annotations available in standard treebanks while reinterpreting them under a more compositional and semantically grounded formalism. As a result, the alignment between syntactic structure and semantic interpretation is significantly improved, making the system highly suitable for unbounded dependency recovery. We evaluate our grammar and reannotation method on an established unbounded dependency recovery task, building upon existing benchmarks by Rimell et al. (2009) and Nivre et al. (2010). Through this evaluation, we demonstrate that our system produces accurate and coherent dependency structures across a wide range of syntactic constructions, particularly those involving unbounded argument movement and roles.

Open Information Extraction (Open IE) is a vibrant area of natural language processing that aims to extract general assertions from unstructured text without requiring a fixed schema or predefined vocabulary of target relations (Etzioni et al., 2011; Kolluru et al., 2014). These extracted assertions can be used for a wide range of applications including knowledge base construction, semantic search, question answering, and event extraction. Most Open IE systems work by identifying logical triples of the form (Argument1, Relation, Argument2), where the Relation typically corresponds to a verb phrase or noun phrase. The key distinguishing feature of Open IE compared with traditional Information Extraction is its domain independence, as it does not presuppose a fixed set of relation types to extract. Instead, it seeks to recover a broad range of relations directly from the surface structure of the input text. Open IE systems, while promising, often suffer from a high rate of false positives in the form of uninformative or semantically incoherent extractions. These extractions lack relevance or concrete meaning, such as oversized subject-verb-object triples that are syntactically valid but do not convey useful semantic information. For example, a system may incorrectly extract "Apple produces devices in California" as "Apple is in California," which strips away crucial semantic context. These issues are particularly detrimental in downstream applications, where the utility of extracted information depends on its relevance and verbosity. In this paper, we present REVERB, a new Open IE system that significantly improves the precision of previously state-of-the-art Open IE extractors, including TexTRunner (Banko et al., 2007) and WOE-pos (Clarke et al., 2006). The key innovation of REVERB lies in its incorporation of two simple but effective syntactic and lexical constraints on the verbal expressions of binary relations: (1) filtering out extractions where the verbal predicate is an intransitive or ambiguous verb, and (2) ensuring the extracted relations form coherent and semantically meaningful subject-predicate-object triples by excluding extractions that do not adhere to standard verb argument structures. We show that these constraints, although syntactically based, drastically improve precision without compromising recall. Our experimental results demonstrate that REVERB not only more than doubles the area under the precision-recall curve compared to earlier systems but also produces a high-quality set of extractions—over 30% of REVERB’s output has a precision of 0.8 or higher. These results suggest that even small, principled syntactic and semantic constraints can have a significant impact on the quality of Open IE output.

Neural word embeddings have become a cornerstone in modern natural language processing (NLP), providing compact and meaningful vector representations of words that capture semantic and syntactic relationships within large corpora (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014). Among the most popular approaches are SkipGrams and Global Vectors (GloVe), which learn distributed representations by optimizing objective functions based on word co-occurrence information. These methods typically produce fixed-dimensional embedding spaces, where the choice of embedding size is made prior to training and is fixed for all downstream applications. However, the demand for flexible dimensionality is often underestimated in NLP pipelines. Different tasks—ranging from classification and clustering to language modeling and transfer learning—require varying levels of representational complexity. Embedding spaces that are either over-dimensional or under-dimensional for a given task can lead to inefficiencies in computational resources or suboptimal performance, respectively. Most existing frameworks require researchers and practitioners to retrain or finetune embeddings when a different embedding dimension is needed for a new application or task. This can be computationally costly, especially when working with large corpora, and it is not consistent with the ideals of modularity and reuse in machine learning. To address this gap, we propose a novel approach to neural word embedding methods: right-truncatable neural word embeddings. This method introduces an incremental learning strategy, in which embedding vectors are built iteratively, one dimension at a time, ensuring that the resulting high-dimensional vector contains all the information captured by the corresponding low-dimensional solutions. This design leverages a key theoretical property: any right-truncated version of the embedding vector exactly replicates the embeddings generated by a lower-dimensional model. Consequently, a single embedding vector can be dynamically adapted to fit a wide array of dimensional requirements across diverse linguistic applications. Our right-truncatable embeddings offer a robust and efficient solution for maintaining embedding consistency across variable dimensions and provide an elegant way to decouple embedding training from task-specific requirements for dimensionality. In addition, they enable practitioners to deploy word embeddings more flexibly in complex pipelines where dimensional constraints are either unknown or subject to change. This innovation opens new avenues for the design and deployment of neural models in real-world NLP systems with varying architectural and computational demands. Furthermore, it facilitates the exploration of optimal embedding dimensions via systematic evaluation with minimal retraining overhead.
