Lexical substitution — the task of replacing a source word with a semantically equivalent target word — plays a central role in many natural language processing tasks, including machine translation, text simplification, and paraphrasing. In cross-lingual settings, it becomes particularly challenging to ensure that the meaning, as well as contextual attributes such as sentiment or subjectivity, is preserved across languages. This is important because words often bear different connotations in different cultural and linguistic domains. A subtle shift in subjectivity — from objective to emotional, or from negative to positive — can introduce inconsistencies and reduce the clarity and accuracy of substituted expressions. In this paper, we address the task of   cross-lingual lexical substitution  , focusing on how   word sense subjectivity   can help bridge the gap between semantic similarity and contextual alignment. Specifically, we investigate whether capturing the subjective or objective nature of a word sense in the source language and matching it in the target language can improve substitution quality. This approach is motivated by the intuition that good substitutions must not only be semantically aligned in meaning but also preserve the color of meaning — especially the sentiment or affective component — that conveys how the context is experienced or perceived. We focus on the English-Chinese language pair in two controlled substitution settings. We show empirically that considering word sense subjectivity during substitution significantly improves performance, as measured by both task-specific metrics and human evaluations. Surprisingly, we find that incorporating subjectivity-based filtering alone can achieve performance comparable to models that integrate detailed   word sense disambiguation (WSD)   systems, particularly for words with multiple senses, some of which are subjective and others objective. This implies that a lightweight treatment of subjectivity can approximate the value provided by more complex sense-based approaches in practical substitution scenarios. To achieve this, we build a model that encodes subjectivity at the sense level, using annotated resources such as BabelNet and sentiment lexicons. We leverage parallel corpora to learn cross-lingual semantic correspondences, while introducing a novel weighting mechanism that prioritizes substitutes whose senses align in terms of subjectivity. The results demonstrate that by mapping not only word senses but their affective properties, we can significantly reduce the performance gap between monolingual and cross-lingual lexical substitution systems. Our findings highlight the nuanced role of subjectivity in cross-lingual semantics and suggest a promising direction for building more contextually aware and culturally sensitive cross-lingual NLP systems.

Domain adaptation is a critical challenge in the field of statistical machine translation (SMT), particularly when the desired target domain is relatively small or not available in sufficient quantities to train a high-quality system. This problem arises in numerous practical applications, where domain-specific systems must be developed with minimal in-domain resources—whether for technical, legal, medical, or other specialized use cases. The availability of large general-domain parallel corpora, however, offers a valuable reservoir of data that, if properly utilized, can be adapted to support domain-specific modeling. The key challenge, therefore, lies in identifying and effectively leveraging the most relevant general-domain sentences when training or decoding within a specific domain. In prior work, domain adaptation strategies have typically relied on either manual annotation of in-domain data or on heuristic filtering based on criteria like domain label, keyword matching, or surface-level features. While these techniques have shown some success, they often require extensive in-domain training data or prior domain knowledge, which is not always available. This paper proposes a more systematic and scalable approach to domain adaptation in SMT through the use of  pseudo in-domain data selection . Our method identifies a small subset of sentences from large general-domain corpora that, while not strictly in-domain, are most relevant to the target domain as judged by cross-entropy-based selection criteria. These pseudo in-domain datasets are compact, comprising only about 1% of the original general-domain data, yet they are highly effective in training domain-adapted models. We introduce and compare three domain-relevant sentence selection methods based on variations of cross-entropy estimation. These principles allow for the efficient filtering of general-domain corpora without requiring explicit domain labels or external resources. The selected pseudo in-domain subcorpora are then used to train small but highly performant domain-specific SMT systems. Notably, our experimental results show that these domain-adapted models consistently outperform systems trained on the full general-domain corpus, and even match or exceed the performance of systems trained on true in-domain data in several settings. Moreover, we find that combining the domain-adapted system trained on pseudo in-domain data with a true in-domain model further improves performance. This suggests that accurate domain adaptation can be achieved not only through careful data selection but also through the integration of domain-specific and domain-agnostic components during decoding.

Entity mention recognition is a fundamental task in named entity processing, traditionally focusing on detecting flat, non-overlapping mentions in text. However, in real-world language, it is common for mentions to exhibit complex, nested, or overlapping structures. For example, in the sentence “The president of the United States of America visited Washington, D.C.,” “The president of the United States of America” is a nested mention containing the submention “the United States of America.” Such nested structures complicate the modeling and detection of mentions, as traditional approaches often fail to account for their recursive and hierarchical nature. Existing systems for mention detection typically assume a flat structure and either ignore or handle nested mentions in a post-hoc manner. Addressing this challenge directly, however, requires a method that explicitly models the relationships between mentions at multiple levels of granularity. Recent advances in transition-based parsing have shown promise in modeling hierarchical and compositional syntactic structures, such as those in dependency parsing and constituency parsing. These frameworks, based on deterministic action sequences, are inherently scalable and capable of modeling ordered, recursive constructions. Building on these insights, this paper introduces a novel neural transition-based approach for nested mention recognition that explicitly accounts for the tree-like structure of mentions in a sentence. Our model formulates the task as a sequence of shift-reduce actions, in which a system incrementally builds a forest-like structure where each node represents a candidate mention. This forest structure captures not only individual mentions but also their nesting relationships. The system processes the sentence in a bottom-up manner, ensuring that the maximal number of transitions required for a sentence of length  n  is bounded to 3 n , a critical factor for scalability and practical deployment. To represent the dynamic state of the parser, we employ a   Stack-LSTM  , a variant of the long short-term memory network designed to model sequential stack-based structures. This allows the system to maintain a continuous and context-sensitive representation of the stack and buffer states during transition. Additionally, we incorporate a   character-based neural component   to capture subword and morphological patterns, which is particularly useful for handling out-of-vocabulary words and detecting mentions in diverse domains. The model is trained using gold-standard mention spans, learning to predict accurate nested structures over time. We evaluate our approach on the widely used ACE (Automated Content Extraction) datasets, which contain richly annotated nested mentions.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has long benefited from the design and integration of feature functions that reflect linguistic properties, alignment behaviors, and domain-specific characteristics of source and target phrase pairs. In traditional SMT frameworks, especially in phrase-based systems, the performance heavily depends on carefully engineered features that are often designed based on linguistic intuition, domain expertise, and iterative model tuning. While these features have proven effective over time, they are limited in their ability to capture high-level semantic information and contextual similarities that are essential for robust translation modeling. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in leveraging deep learning for SMT, motivated by the success of neural networks in tasks like speech recognition, image classification, and language modeling. However, the integration of deep learning models into the feature-rich paradigm of statistical translation poses numerous challenges, particularly in terms of scalability, interpretability, and the ability to utilize both labeled and unlabeled data effectively. This paper introduces a novel semi-supervised deep auto-encoder (DAE) feature learning approach for enhancing the phrase-based translation model in SMT. Unlike traditional feature engineering, where features are crafted heuristically, we propose directly learning new and effective features using the deep auto-encoder architecture. Our approach takes two core steps: pre-training and fine-tuning. First, we pre-train a deep belief network (DBN) in an unsupervised manner using a large corpus of unlabeled data, and use these pre-trained parameters as the initial weights for the DAE. This initialization step allows the DAE to start from a meaningful representation space, which improves convergence during the subsequent supervised phase. Next, we perform semi-supervised fine-tuning using a limited amount of labeled translation data, where the original phrase features from the translation model act as a  teacher  signal to guide the learning process. This enables the DAE to learn feature representations that are not only semantically rich but also aligned with the translation task at hand. Beyond the basic DAE framework, we further introduce a horizontal composition of multiple DAEs for deeper representation learning. By stacking more DAE layers with large hidden units, we enable the model to learn high-dimensional non-linear features that can capture subtle dependencies between source and target phrases. This hierarchical learning of features leads to a more discriminative and generalizable feature space, which is critical for improving translation accuracy, particularly in low-resource or out-of-domain scenarios.

Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved the performance of dialogue systems in generating relevant and coherent responses. Among various techniques, sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models have become dominant in response generation, due to their ability to learn long-range dependencies in dialogue data. However, the conventional Seq2Seq approach, particularly when trained via maximum-likelihood estimation, often suffers from the so-called “safe response” phenomenon, where the model tend to generate generic and non-informative responses that avoid semantic risks. This problem is especially evident in single-turn, short-text conversation scenarios where the model must generate concise and meaningful replies based on minimal input. To address this challenge, the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework has been explored as a promising alternative for training dialogue models that generate more engaging and diverse responses. In a GAN setup, a generative model is simultaneously trained with a discriminative model: the generator learns to produce realistic dialogue responses, while the discriminator is trained to distinguish between human-like responses and machine-generated ones. This adversarial training process helps the generator to avoid producing trivial or repetitive responses, resulting in outputs that are more contextually grounded and semantically rich. In this paper, we propose a neural response generation framework that combines the strengths of GANs and the Seq2Seq paradigm, with a specific focus on short-text dialogue generation in both Mandarin and English languages. A major challenge in training GANs with Seq2Seq models is the non-differentiable nature of the decoding process, which prevents the use of gradient-based optimization in the generator. To tackle this issue, we introduce an approximate embedding layer that enables the gradient to flow through the discrete output sequences, thereby making the training process end-to-end differentiable and compatible with adversarial learning techniques. Our proposed model is evaluated on widely used dialogue datasets in both Mandarin and English. The results demonstrate that the integration of GAN and an approximate embedding layer leads to significant improvements in response diversity, as measured by standard evaluation metrics such as distinct n-grams. Additionally, the response relevance, often considered at odds with diversity, is only slightly impacted, further validating the effectiveness of the approach. This work contributes to the broader theme of improving the conversational quality of neural dialogue systems by leveraging adversarial learning to push the boundaries of traditional response generation models. By addressing the non-differentiability problem inherent in the Seq2Seq decoding process, the proposed method paves the way for more dynamic and human-like responses in practical dialogue systems.

Grammar induction techniques have grown to be a crucial component in natural language processing, especially in scenarios where annotated resources for a target language are limited or non-existent. Dependency grammar, in particular, has attracted significant attention due to its widespread use in syntactic parsing systems. While supervised methods for dependency parsing achieve high accuracy when trained on sufficiently annotated corpora, these methods are unsuitable for low-resource languages where such data is unavailable. In response to this challenge, a number of unsupervised and semi-supervised grammar induction approaches have been developed. Unsupervised methods typically rely on the statistical regularities in monolingual text to infer the underlying syntactic structure. While effective to some extent, these methods often struggle to reach the performance levels achieved by supervised systems and can fail to capture complex dependency patterns, particularly in languages with high morphological variability or rich syntactic structure. On the other hand, bilingual projection techniques offer a promising alternative by leveraging syntactic information from a closely related or resource-rich language. These approaches transfer syntactic structures through alignment with a parallel corpus, effectively bootstrapping the grammar induction process for the target language. However, such methods heavily rely on the quality of alignment and the syntactic similarity between the source and target languages. This can lead to errors in the projected structures and result in suboptimal performance, particularly when the alignment is imperfect or when the languages are typologically distant. Furthermore, such approaches often neglect the linguistic idiosyncrasies present in the target language, as the projected grammatical structures are largely shaped by the source language's syntactic conventions. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel strategy for the induction of a monolingual dependency grammar that utilizes a dual approach: combining the strengths of bilingual projection and unsupervised learning. Specifically, the proposed method is guided by the dependency information projected from a source language (typically English, the most resource-rich language in many domains) and simultaneously learns the native syntactic structure of the target language using unsupervised techniques. This bilingually-guided strategy enhances the grammatical structure induction process by aligning with the syntactic patterns present in the source language while being sensitive to the target language's own syntactic properties. As a result, the method achieves a more accurate and linguistically appropriate monolingual dependency grammar than either bilingual projection or unsupervised induction alone. Experiments on a set of five structurally and typologically diverse languages demonstrate the effectiveness of this hybrid strategy.

The task of identifying and recommending anecdotes is a novel and underexplored challenge in natural language processing (NLP) with real-world implications for education, argumentation, and content curation. An anecdote, by definition, is a concise and often narrative-like account of an individual’s experience that serves a broader contextual or thematic purpose. Typically found in argumentative or persuasive writing, anecdotes are powerful rhetorical devices that support claims by providing concrete, relatable examples. Their effective use, however, often depends on the availability of relevant and impactful stories. This paper introduces the task of   Anecdote Recognition and Recommendation  —the process of identifying anecdotes within written texts and recommending them to users based on given topics or themes. In this work, we propose representing an anecdote in a structured manner as a tuple: `< person, story, implication >`. The  person  is the subject of the anecdote, the  story  consists of the events or sequence described, and the  implication  is the underlying message or thematic insight derived from the narrative. This structure not only helps in organizing anecdotal information but also enables deeper analysis and relevance assessment for recommendation tasks. Our approach is rooted in the analysis of argumentative essays, where anecdotes are embedded within the discourse as supporting evidence. To extract anecdotes, we leverage   discourse role identification  , a method used to recognize the roles played by sentences within a document such as  thesis ,  main idea , and  support . By identifying the  support  role, we locate potential anecdotes and extract the  story . The greater challenge lies in uncovering the  implication , which captures the deeper meaning or topic associated with the anecdote. To this end, we employ semantic and contextual analysis techniques to derive these implications accurately. Experiments using archived collections of argumentative essays demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Our system not only successfully identifies informative and interpretable anecdotes but also recommends them in response to given topics. The empirical results highlight the crucial role of anecdote implications in bridging user interests with relevant anecdotes. For instance, anecdotes expressing implications related to resilience, perseverance, or innovation are shown to be particularly effective when recommended under related thematic inputs. This work opens new research avenues in the area of content-based recommendation systems and academically supported argument extraction. By formalizing the anecdote as a structured unit, we provide a scalable and interpretable model that can support the development of intelligent tools for argumentative writing, educational aids, and personalized content discovery.

Semi-supervised learning has proven to be an effective strategy for improving performance in a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly in scenarios where labeled data is scarce or costly to obtain. In the context of sequence labeling, such as named entity recognition or part-of-speech tagging, the challenge is to leverage both the limited amount of labeled examples and the abundant unlabeled data to learn robust and generalizable sequence representations. Most traditional semi-supervised methods rely heavily on heuristics, such as self-training or pseudo-labeling, to iteratively refine predictions and augment the training set. However, these approaches often lack a principled model of the underlying data distribution and struggle to make optimal use of unlabeled data. In this paper, we introduce a novel family of variational sequential labelers that enable principled semi-supervised learning for sequence labeling tasks via the integration of a generative and a discriminative component. Our approach is built upon a multitask framework where we explicitly model the joint probability of both the observed words and their corresponding labels. The core idea is to use latent variables, inspired by those used in modern language modeling and word embedding methods like BERT or Word2Vec, to capture context-aware representations of words and their dependencies. These latent variables play a dual role: they define the conditional distribution of a word given its context (a task akin to masked language modeling) and simultaneously provide a rich shared representation between the generative and discriminative components of the model. A crucial advantage of our method is its use of hierarchical latent variable structures, which allow the model to disentangle information at multiple levels of abstraction. Specifically, the latent variables can be designed to encode both word-specific and label-specific factors, enabling the model to learn more discriminative representations that generalize well to new, unseen sequences. This hierarchical structure also enables the model to bridge the gap between the prediction of individual words and the overall task of sequence labeling, making it easier to transfer discriminative knowledge from the label space into the latent space. The variational inference framework provides a flexible and principled approach for optimizing the joint objective by maximizing a lower bound on the marginal likelihood of both labeled and unlabeled data. This allows our model to make full use of the unlabeled data while maintaining strong performance on explicitly labeled examples. Through extensive experiments on eight diverse sequence labeling datasets, we demonstrate that our variational sequential labelers consistently outperform strong baseline models, including both fully supervised and semi-supervised approaches.

Morphological analysis is a foundational task in natural language processing, enabling a wide range of downstream applications such as syntactic parsing, machine translation, and text normalization. While morphological analysis is relatively straightforward in languages with clear word boundaries, such as English or German, it poses a significant challenge in unsegmented languages like Japanese, Chinese, and Thai, where there is no clear separation between words and morphemes at the character level. In these languages, segmentation is typically a necessary preprocessing step before morphological analysis, and conventional methods rely on either rule-based systems or statistical models trained on hand-annotated corpora. However, the use of automatically segmented data introduces noise into the process, as segmentation errors propagate through subsequent linguistic stages and affect the accuracy of morphological analysis. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly recurrent neural network language models (RNNLMs), offer promising avenues for addressing these limitations. RNNLMs are particularly well-suited for sequence modeling tasks and are capable of learning complex patterns in sequential data, including context-dependent representations of word sequences. Traditional language models, however, often treat word ordering as a discrete and rigid constraint, making them less effective in scenarios involving noisy or ambiguous data. In this paper, we propose a novel morphological analysis framework that leverages the semantic contextualization strength of RNNLMs to improve the accuracy of morphological tagging in unsegmented languages. The key insight of our approach lies in the integration of semantic plausibility into the morphological analysis pipeline. Rather than relying solely on segmentation-based surface-level features, our model uses the RNNLM's ability to capture the contextual meaning of word sequences. This allows the model to infer the most semantically likely morphological tags, even when the underlying segmentation is imperfect. Unlike conventional approaches that treat segmentation and tagging as separate and sequential tasks, our model learns a joint representation that aligns the prediction of morphological tags with a globally coherent semantic structure. To evaluate the effectiveness of our model, we conduct extensive experiments on two Japanese corpora. Japanese is an ideal test case for our method due to its complex and context-sensitive morphological system, where word boundaries are ambiguous and heavily influenced by grammatical function and syntactic dependency. Our proposed model achieves significant improvements over baseline approaches, demonstrating the efficacy of integrating semantic plausibility from RNNLMs into morphological analysis for unsegmented languages. These results highlight the importance of incorporating higher-level linguistic representations in tasks traditionally rooted in surface-level processing.

Document segmentation is a key task in natural language processing, enabling better comprehension, summarisation, and retrieval of textual content by decomposing a document into thematically coherent parts. Although much research has focused on flat, single-level segmenters that categorise document content into uniform thematic segments, the structure of many documents — particularly those in academic, journalistic, or long-form writing — often reveals a hierarchical organisation, where macro-topics are further subdivided into more specific subtopics. This necessitates a segmenter that can not only identify main topic transitions but also uncover nested or localised thematic shifts within these broader sections. Such hierarchical topical segmentation can be particularly valuable in improving information structuring, enhancing readability, and facilitating deeper semantic understanding of complex texts. Traditional segmentation methods typically require a fixed number of segments to be specified in advance — a limitation that hinders their applicability to real-world documents whose structural complexity is not known a priori. Furthermore, iteratively assembling a hierarchical segmentation by running several levels of single-segmenters has proven suboptimal due to incompatibility between the different levels of granularity and inconsistency in segmentation boundaries resulting from the non-hierarchical nature of the underlying models. In this paper, we present   Hierarchical Affinity Propagation for Segmentation (HAPS)  , a novel approach to hierarchical topical segmentation inspired by the Affinity Propagation (AP) clustering algorithm. HAPS takes as input a document and recursively partitions it into segments, building a tree-like structure where the root node captures the most prominent topic shift and deeper nodes represent increasingly finer thematic boundaries. Each segment in the tree is also accompanied by a representative "segment centre" — a key sentence or paragraph that best encapsulates the theme of that particular segment — aiding in interpretation and summarisation. HAPS is designed to avoid the key limitations of existing techniques. It requires no prior specification of the number of segments and can naturally model documents with varying degrees of hierarchical complexity. Moreover, by leveraging the message-passing mechanism of Affinity Propagation, HAPS identifies cluster exemplars (i.e., segment centres) that are contextually representative and linguistically salient. This enables the model to generalise across different text genres and document structures without requiring domain-specific feature engineering. We evaluate HAPS on two datasets: a manually segmented corpus annotated by multiple annotators to assess human-consistent segmentation quality, and a collection of Wikipedia articles, which serve as a real-world benchmark for testing on unstructured, long-form texts.

Interpreting anaphoric shell nouns (ASNs), such as "this issue" or "this fact," is a crucial task in natural language understanding, often serving as a bridge to maintain coherence and referential clarity across discourse. These nominal expressions appear frequently in texts and are used to refer back to a previously mentioned or contextually accessible event or situation. However, the automated interpretation of ASNs remains a formidable challenge due to the ambiguities in their meaning and the absence of direct contextual antecedents that are typically present in ordinary anaphora resolution tasks. This difficulty is exacerbated by the paucity of annotated datasets that capture the full spectrum of ASN antecedents, making it arduous to train robust and generalizable models suitable for large-scale textual analysis. The crux of the problem lies in identifying an appropriate antecedent for an ASN, which is often an event or fact stated in the text or implied by the discourse context. For instance, an ASN like "this conclusion" must be linked to a previously formulated or contextually relevant proposition. This task becomes especially complex when the antecedent is implicit or non-referential, or when the ASN is embedded within complex syntactic structures that mask its relationship to the antecedent. One insight that has emerged from linguistic and computational studies is the potential of using cataphoric shell nouns (CSNs), such as "the fact that X," as a complementary data source for addressing the interpretation challenge of ASNs. CSNs often serve to introduce or highlight their own antecedents, making them particularly transparent in terms of meaning. They provide a relatively unambiguous and easily interpretable counterpart to the otherwise opaque ASNs. By leveraging the structure and semantics of CSNs, we can exploit these rich and underutilized linguistic resources to train models for interpreting ASNs without requiring annotated ASN antecedents. This paper proposes a novel approach to automatically interpret ASNs by utilizing the antecedents of CSNs as training data. Our method extracts antecedents of CSNs from corpora and uses them to train models that can infer the corresponding meanings of ASNs. This strategy not only circumvents the need for costly ASN-specific annotations but also capitalizes on the inherent clarity and structure of CSNs to bootstrap the learning process. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with the proposed model achieving precision scores ranging from 0.35 (baseline = 0.21) to 0.72 (baseline = 0.44) across different shell nouns. These results underscore the potential of using CSNs as a training resource for interpreting ASNs and offer a promising path toward developing scalable and data-efficient methods for anaphora resolution in natural language processing.

Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) is a highly expressive formalism for modeling the syntax and semantics of natural language. It captures complex syntactic phenomena such as long-range dependencies and complex heads, making it suitable for robust and accurate parsing systems. Despite its computational and descriptive power, constructing large CCG treebanks is a costly and labor-intensive task. This has led to significant research interest in unsupervised methods for inducing CCG grammars from raw text corpora. While early work laid a promising foundation, modeling lexical information and capturing grammatical structure effectively remain challenging problems in the unsupervised induction of CCGs. In this paper, we introduce two key methodological improvements to the unsupervised induction of CCG grammars, building on the baseline model presented by Bisk and Hockenmaier (2012). First, we investigate the use of boundary part-of-speech (POS) tags to enrich the lexical prior of the grammar induction model. These boundary POS tags provide valuable clues about word usage context in sentence boundaries and help the model differentiate between syntactic roles even in the absence of explicit phrase structure. We hypothesize that incorporating such fine-grained lexical information can reduce ambiguity and improve the alignment of words with grammars during the induction process. Second, we propose to replace the traditional maximum likelihood estimation with a nonparametric Bayesian approach based on the Pitman-Yor process (PYP). Unlike fixed-state models, PYP allows the number of grammar categories to grow as needed with the data, ensuring flexibility and scalability. This Bayesian formulation not only improves the robustness of the learned grammar but also encourages the discovery of a compact and generalizable rule set. We derive a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference procedure using Gibbs sampling to estimate the model parameters efficiently. We evaluate our proposed methods on the English Penn Treebank, a widely used resource for syntactic evaluations. Our experiments demonstrate that the integration of boundary POS tags leads to a notable improvement in parsing accuracy and grammar quality over the baseline. Furthermore, the use of Bayesian inference based on the Pitman-Yor process results in more compact and generalizable grammars without sacrificing performance. Together, these two enhancements address key limitations of existing models and propose a promising direction for improving the scalability and effectiveness of unsupervised CCG induction. By demonstrating that additional lexical signals and informed probabilistic modeling can significantly improve the learning of combinatorial grammars from unannotated text, our work contributes to the broader goal of developing data-efficient and accurate syntactic parsing systems for natural language processing.

Recent years have witnessed rapid advancements in neural machine translation (NMT), with claims of significant progress toward—and in some cases even achieving—human parity in translation quality. Among the most notable assertions is that NMT systems have reached parity with professional human translators on specific tasks, such as the WMT Chinese-English news translation task. These claims are primarily based on evaluations conducted at the sentence level using well-established benchmarks and human evaluation protocols. However, as translation systems become more sophisticated, subtle differences in performance—such as coherence, consistency, and referential accuracy—are increasingly influenced by document-level phenomena. These are often masked when evaluation is restricted to the sentence level. In this paper, we critically examine the recent claims of human parity in NMT by advocating for a broader perspective in system evaluation. Specifically, we argue that sentence-level metrics and evaluations are insufficient when systems approach the performance ceiling of human-level translation, and that document-level evaluation is essential to capture the full picture of translation quality. We conduct a large-scale human evaluation experiment in which raters assess the adequacy and fluency of machine and human translations, comparing results for both isolated sentences and entire documents. Our findings reveal that when translations are evaluated at the document level, human raters consistently show a stronger preference for human translations over machine translations than when judging sentences in isolation. These results suggest that, while machine translation may match human performance on individual sentences, it still lags behind in capturing and maintaining the larger context and coherence necessary for high-quality document-level translation. The implications of our findings are significant. First, they highlight that the standard benchmarking practices used in machine translation research may fail to reflect the true capabilities of modern NMT systems, especially when evaluating against professional human performance. Second, as NMT systems improve and errors at the sentence level become fewer or indistinguishable, document-level phenomena—such as discourse structure, consistency of terminology, and anaphora resolution—emerge as critical differentiators in quality. Therefore, we argue that future research in machine translation must incorporate document-level evaluation as a core part of performance assessment. By shifting the focus from sentence-level evaluation to document-level analysis, the research community can gain deeper insights into the current limitations of NMT and guide the development of more context-aware and coherent translation systems. This paper contributes a new experimental protocol based on document-level human evaluation and advocates for its adoption in future research and development efforts.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable success in recent years, especially for high-resource language pairs where large parallel corpora are available to train deep encoder-decoder architectures (Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2015). However, the performance of NMT on low-resource language pairs, particularly when one of the languages is rare (e.g., has minimal available data), remains a significant challenge. The lack of abundant and high-quality bilingual data leads to poor model generalization and underfitting, impeding the translation of underrepresented languages in multilingual setups (Zhang et al., 2019). To address this issue, researchers have explored various methods such as transfer learning (Cho et al., 2019), multilingual training (Wu & Mackey, 2017), and back-translation (Sennrich et al., 2016). However, these approaches often fall short when dealing with pairs in which at least one language remains extremely underrepresented, such as the pair (X, Z) where Z is a rare language. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for addressing rare language translation through a  triangular architecture  (TA-NMT), which introduces an auxiliary rich language Y to form a triangle of language relationships between languages X, Y, and Z. The core idea centers on leveraging the strengths of the existing (X, Y) and (Y, Z) translation systems to improve the (X, Z) translation task. Our approach is particularly useful in scenarios where the (X, Y) pair is well-resourced, while the (X, Z) and (Y, Z) pairs suffer from data scarcity. In our triangular architecture, Z is treated as an intermediate latent variable, enabling the joint optimization of different translation models under a unified bidirectional Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework. The EM-based optimization aims to maximize the likelihood of translation for the (X, Y) pair while simultaneously improving (X, Z) translation by utilizing minimal (X, Z) and (Y, Z) data. This approach allows the model to implicitly learn latent representations that are aligned across all three languages, with special emphasis on the rare language Z. Notably, our work represents a departure from the traditional chain-based or pivot-based translation methods that go through a single pivot language, as our triangular architecture ensures bidirectional and symmetrical optimization, making the system more robust in low-resource conditions. By treating rare language translation as a latent variable learning problem, we also offer a principled way to integrate rich knowledge from high-resource languages without explicitly requiring massive bilingual data for every pair.

Entity linking (EL), also known as named entity disambiguation, is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that aims to identify and link mentions of entities in text to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base (KB), such as Wikipedia or Freebase. This task is particularly challenging due to the ambiguity of named entities that may refer to multiple different entities in the KB, depending on the context. For example, "Apple" could refer to the company, the fruit, or a brand of computer. Accurately resolving such ambiguities is crucial for a variety of downstream applications, including question answering, information extraction, and semantic search. Traditional approaches to entity linking typically leverage surface forms, neighboring words, or static dictionaries to identify the correct entity among candidate mentions. More recently, methods have also explored the use of contextual information, either by directly modeling the mention co-occurring words or by integrating external world knowledge. However, assembling a robust EL system requires better exploitation of both local contextual information and global world knowledge to enrich the relevance scores between the text mention and candidate KB entities. In this paper, we present a novel approach to entity linking that combines a statistical language model-based information retrieval framework with query expansion techniques. Inspired by the well-established framework in information retrieval (IR), we model the matching between the local context of the entity mention and the set of candidate KB entities as a query-document retrieval problem. To enhance the effectiveness of this matching, we incorporate query expansion strategies that expand the original query using both the local co-occurring context and extracted world knowledge. A distinctive feature of our approach is the emphasis placed on named entities within the local context. These entities are treated as informative signals and are weighted differently using a positional language model, which accounts for their relative distances to the query mention. We evaluate our method on the TAC-KBP 2010 dataset, a widely used benchmark for entity linking and entity disambiguation. Our experiments demonstrate that the integration of local contextual and global world knowledge through query expansion techniques leads to significant improvements in disambiguating named entities. The system effectiveness is measured using standard EL evaluation metrics such as accuracy and precision, and our performance compares favorably to the official results reported by participants of the KBP 2010 task. This work contributes to the field of entity linking by introducing a principled approach that combines local and global context through probabilistic language modeling with query expansion, and by providing a competitive solution for entity disambiguation without relying on computationally expensive deep learning architectures.

Chinese evaluative information analysis has become a crucial research area in natural language processing, especially with the explosive growth of Chinese online content such as social media, news, and reviews. This deluge of textual data provides an unprecedented opportunity to analyze public opinions, sentiments, and attitudes toward various topics, products, services, or events. Evaluative information—information expressing subjective evaluations, emotions, or judgments—forms the backbone of this analysis. It encompasses not only sentiment (positive, negative, neutral) but also a rich spectrum of evaluative expressions, including degrees, modality, and complex syntactic constructions. Hence, analyzing Chinese evaluative information is not only a task of quantifying sentiment but also of understanding the nuanced and context-sensitive nature of the language, which is especially challenging in Chinese due to its morphological and syntactic features. In this paper, we present the Chinese Evaluative Information Analyzer (CEIA), a system designed to extract and analyze a broader and more diverse set of evaluative elements than previous systems aimed at Chinese text. Our approach is grounded in a comprehensive definition of evaluative information that integrates attitudes, sentiments, and opinions in a unified theoretical framework. The CEIA aims to move beyond simple sentiment classification and instead captures the multifaceted nature of evaluation as expressed in Chinese texts. For instance, while prior work often focuses on extracting opinion targets and aspect-level sentiments from reviews, we consider constructing a system that can handle implicit evaluative cues, multi-word evaluative expressions, and nuanced sentiments expressed in more complex syntactic and semantic structures. To achieve this, we make three major contributions in this paper. First, we introduce CEIA, a system that is designed to extract a richer and more diverse set of evaluative elements from Chinese texts than previous systems. Second, to support the development and evaluation of CEIA, we have created a large-scale annotated corpus specifically for the task of Chinese evaluative information analysis. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first corpus of its kind that includes not only annotated sentiment polarities but also rich syntactic and semantic attributes expressing evaluation. Third, we propose novel feature types including syntactic dependency paths, semantic classes of words, and contextual distance measures to enhance the extraction of evaluative expressions. These features are designed to capture the subtle dependencies and relationships that influence the interpretation of evaluative information in Chinese text. To validate the effectiveness of these contributions, we conduct a series of experiments on our annotated corpus.

The task of learning meaningful distributed representations of words is central to many natural language processing applications. A promising approach for this task is the skip-gram model (Mikolov et al., 2013a), which learns vector representations for words based on the distributional properties of their co-occurring context words. While these representations capture rich semantic relationships, they assume that each word corresponds to a single vector regardless of polysemy — a simplification that breaks down for words with multiple meanings. To address this limitation, numerous approaches have proposed multi-sense word embeddings (Arora et al., 2016; Faruqui and Mansinghka, 2016; Hill et al., 2016; Neubig and Hu, 2018), where each word is associated with multiple representations corresponding to its different senses. Despite their theoretical appeal, many multi-sense models are either non-differentiable — requiring discrete sense annotations as input — or complex in design, which hinders their interpretation and scalability. We present the  disambiguated skip-gram model , a neural-probabilistic framework for learning multi-sense distributed word representations in an end-to-end manner. Like the original skip-gram model, our approach is based on the distributional hypothesis: the meaning of a word is related to the words that surround it. However, while traditional skip-gram assigns a single context-specific vector to each word, the disambiguated skip-gram jointly learns both the context prediction model and an internal sense disambiguation mechanism. This allows us to model the multiple meanings of a word explicitly within the architecture, without requiring annotated sense labels at either training or inference time. The model is differentiable end-to-end, enabling fully optimized training and eliminating the need for external sense taggers or the iterative sense prediction models common in most multi-sense approaches. An important property of the disambiguated skip-gram model is its neural interpretation. The model can be viewed as a simple feed-forward neural network, with the hidden layers corresponding to the sense selection mechanism and the output layer comprising context word predictions. This makes the model both tractable and analyzable. Additionally, to increase practical usefulness, we introduce a novel  pruning strategy  for the embeddings generated by the model. This strategy allows us to control the complexity of the representation space, reducing the number of sense vectors while preserving the most informative ones for downstream tasks. We evaluate the disambiguated skip-gram model on several widely used word sense induction benchmarks. Our results indicate that the model achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets, surpassing previous multi-sense models and even outperforming single-sense baselines in certain cases.

Conversational systems have become a core technology in human-computer interaction, with applications ranging from customer service chatbots to personal assistants like Alexa and Google Assistant. While progress in this field has largely been driven by data-intensive machine learning techniques, particularly for specialized domains with limited discourse ranges, the development of open-domain conversational systems capable of engaging in natural, flowing conversations remains a significant challenge. Traditional approaches often fall short in maintaining coherence and flexibility over extended interactions with widely varying topics. Early systems typically relied on human-crafted rules or pre-defined dialogue templates, which, although effective in maintaining clarity and structure, require extensive manual labor and are difficult to scale. More recent efforts have focused on data-driven methods, especially retrieval-based and generative models, which promise scalability and adaptability but often at the cost of reduced naturalness and coherence. This paper addresses the challenges of building an open-domain conversational system by proposing a novel architecture composed entirely of modules grounded in natural language processing (NLP) techniques, without relying on rule-based components or retrieval from predefined response corpora. Our approach moves beyond traditional pipeline systems, where each component is optimized in isolation, by integrating tasks such as dialogue state tracking, response generation, and discourse modeling into a tightly coordinated framework. A core innovation of this architecture is the use of contextualized language understanding and generative models that are fine-tuned for dialogue continuity and user engagement, ensuring that the system can maintain long, contextually rich conversations across a wide range of topics. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we implemented the proposed architecture and conducted user studies comparing it to two baseline systems: a retrieval-based system and a rule-based system with a large scale of 149K manually crafted rules. The results of the experiments demonstrate that our NLP-based architecture significantly outperforms the retrieval baseline in terms of naturalness while achieving a level of interaction quality that is comparable to the rule-based system. This finding not only highlights the potential of end-to-end NLP techniques in conversational systems but also suggests that future open-domain dialogue systems can be built more efficiently by minimizing dependence on manual rule engineering.
